arXiv:1007.5508v1 [math.NT] 30 Jul 2010

Rings and ideals parametrized by binary nn-ic forms

Melanie Matchett Wood ††thanks: mwood@math.stanford.edu Affiliation: Stanford University, Department of Mathematics, Affiliation: Building 380, Sloan Hall, Affiliation: Stanford, California 94305
Abstract

The association of algebraic objects to forms has had many important applications in number theory. Gauss, over two centuries ago, studied quadratic rings and ideals associated to binary quadratic forms, and found that ideal classes of quadratic rings are exactly parametrized by equivalence classes of integral binary quadratic forms. Delone and Faddeev, in 1940, showed that cubic rings are parametrized by equivalence classes of integral binary cubic forms. Birch, Merriman, Nakagawa, Corso, Dvornicich, and Simon have all studied rings associated to binary forms of degree nn for any nn, but it has not previously been known which rings, and with what additional structure, are associated to binary forms.

In this paper, we show exactly what algebraic structures are parametrized by binary nn-ic forms, for all nn. The algebraic data associated to an integral binary nn-ic form includes a ring isomorphic to ℤn{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} as a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module, an ideal class for that ring, and a condition on the ring and ideal class that comes naturally from geometry. In fact, we prove these parametrizations when any base scheme replaces the integers, and show that the correspondences between forms and the algebraic data are functorial in the base scheme. We give geometric constructions of the rings and ideals from the forms that parametrize them and a simple construction of the form from an appropriate ring and ideal.

1 Introduction

When one looks for a parametrizing space for degree nn number fields, binary nn-ic forms are a natural guess. It turns out that for n=3n=3 this guess is correct. We have that GL2⁡(ℚ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}({\mathbb{Q}}) classes of binary cubic forms with rational coefficients are in bijection with isomorphism classes of cubic ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-algebras and irreducible forms correspond to cubic number fields. Moreover, an analogous result allows the parametrization of orders in those number fields; GL2⁡(ℤ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}}) classes of integral binary cubic forms are in bijection with isomorphism classes of cubic rings ([8], see also [5], [9], [2]). For other nn, the space of binary nn-ic forms parametrizes algebraic data that is more subtle than this. It has long been known that binary quadratic forms parametrize ideal classes in quadratic rings (originally in [10], see [20], [14], or [22] for a modern treatment). In this paper, we construct the algebraic data associated to a binary nn-ic form, and determine what algebraic structures are in fact parametrized by binary nn-ic forms for all nn.

Every binary nn-ic form with integral coefficients does have an associated ring. The rings that come from binary nn-ic forms are interesting for many reasons in their own right, in particular because we have several other tools to understand these rings. Del Corso, Dvornicich, and Simon have viewed the rings associated to binary nn-ic forms as a generalization of monogenic rings and have described how a prime splits in a ring associated to a binary nn-ic form in terms of the factorization of the form modulo the prime [6]. They have also given a condition on the form equivalent to the pp-maximality of the associated ring. Simon [19] uses the ring associated to a binary form to find a class group obstruction equations of the form C​yd=f⁡(x,y)Cy^{d}=f(x,y) having integral solutions (where ff is the binary form). Work of the author finds an explicit moduli space for ideal classes in the rings associated to binary nn-ic forms [23]. Thus, we can work explicitly with these rings, prime splitting in them, and their ideal classes.

However, in addition to the ring that is canonically associated to a binary form, there is more associated data, including ideal classes of the ring. Some of these ideal classes have been constructed for irreducible, primitive forms in [18], [6], and [19]. In Section 2, we give four different ways to construct the associated ring and ideal classes from a binary form 1) explicitly as a subring of a ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-algebra, 2) by giving the multiplication and action tables, 3) via a simple geometric construction that works when f≢0f\not\equiv 0, and 4) via a more complicated geometric construction that works in all cases. The geometric constructions answer a question posed by Lenstra at the Lorentz Center Rings of Low Rank Workshop in 2006 about giving a basis-free description of the ring associated to a binary form. In the case n=3n=3, the geometric construction of 4) was originally given in a letter of Deligne [7]. We see that for n≠2n\neq 2 the ring associated to a form is Gorenstein if and only if the form is primitive. Also, the ideal classes associated to the form are invertible if and only if the form is primitive. The geometric construction of a ring and ideal classes from a binary form is so simple that we give it here.

A binary nn-ic form with integer coefficients describes a subscheme of ℙℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}} which we call Sf{S_{f}}. Let 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k) denote the usual sheaf on ℙℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}} and let 𝒪Sf​(k)\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k) denote its pullback to Sf{S_{f}}. Also, for a sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F}, let Γ⁡(ℱ)\Gamma(\mathcal{F}) be the global sections of ℱ\mathcal{F}. When f≢0f\not\equiv 0, the ring associated to the binary nn-ic form ff is simply the ring of global functions of Sf{S_{f}}. The global sections Γ​(𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}(k)) have an Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}})-module structure, and for a binary form f≢0f\not\equiv 0 and −1≤k≤n−1-1\leq k\leq n-1, the global sections Γ​(𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}(k)) give a module of the ring associated to ff which is realizable as an ideal class. When n=2n=2, taking k=1k=1 we obtain the ideal associated to the binary quadratic form in Gauss composition. (This construction gives an ideal even when ff is reducible or non-primitive. See [22] for a complete description of the n=2n=2 case.) When n=3n=3, we expect to obtain canonical modules for the ring since we know binary cubic forms parametrize exactly cubic rings. When n=3n=3, by taking k=1k=1 we obtain the inverse different of the ring associated to the binary cubic form, and in general taking k=n−2k=n-2 gives the inverse different (see Theorem 2.4). Thus from a binary form, we naturally construct a ring and several ideal classes. As we are interested in understanding exactly what data is parametrized by binary forms, the natural questions remaining are: is there more data naturally associated to the form? is some of the data we have already constructed redundant, in other words could it be constructed from other pieces of the data? and what rings and ideal classes actual arise from this construction?

First, we will see that there is more important structure to the ring and ideal classes we have constructed. Given a form ff, let RR be the associated ring, and II the ideal from k=n−3k=n-3. From the exact sequences on ℙℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}}

0→𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪→𝒪/f⁡(𝒪⁡(−n))→00\rightarrow\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}/f(\mathcal{O}(-n))\rightarrow 0

and

0→𝒪⁡(−3)→f𝒪⁡(n−3)→𝒪⁡(n−3)/f⁡(𝒪⁡(−3))→00\rightarrow\mathcal{O}(-3)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(n-3)\rightarrow\mathcal{O}(n-3)/f(\mathcal{O}(-3))\rightarrow 0

we obtain exact sequences

0→ℤ→R→H1​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(−n))→00\rightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}\rightarrow R\rightarrow H^{1}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(-n))\rightarrow 0

and

0→H0​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(n−3))→I→H1​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(−3))→0.0\rightarrow H^{0}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(n-3))\rightarrow I\rightarrow H^{1}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(-3))\rightarrow 0.

We have a map R⊗I→IR\otimes I\rightarrow I from the action of the ring on the ideal, and thus a map ϕ:R/ℤ⊗H0​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(n−3))→H1​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(−3))\phi:R/{\mathbb{Z}}\otimes H^{0}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(n-3))\rightarrow H^{1}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(-3)). It is easy to see that with the identification of R/ℤR/{\mathbb{Z}} with H1​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(−n))H^{1}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(-n)), that ϕ\phi is the same as the natural map

H1​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(−n))⊗H0​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(n−3))→H1​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(−3)).H^{1}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(-n))\otimes H^{0}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(n-3))\rightarrow H^{1}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(-3)).

Note if we write V=ℤ2V={\mathbb{Z}}^{2}, then we have OPENH1​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(−n)))=Symn−2⁡V∗H^{1}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(-n)))=\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}V^{*}, and H0​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(n−3))=Symn−3⁡VH^{0}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(n-3))=\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}V, and H1​(ℙℤ1,𝒪⁡(−3))=V∗H^{1}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}},\mathcal{O}(-3))=V^{*}.

In Section 4, we prove that the above algebraic data is precisely the data parametrized by binary nn-ic forms.

Theorem 1.1.

Given a ring RR and an RR-module II, we have that RR and II are associated to a binary nn-ic form if and only if we can write R/ℤ=Symn−2⁡V∗R/{\mathbb{Z}}=\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}V^{*} and an exact sequence 0→Symn−3⁡V→I→V∗→00\rightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}V\rightarrow I\rightarrow V^{*}\rightarrow 0 such that the map Symn−2⁡V∗⊗Symn−3⁡V→V∗\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}V^{*}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}V\rightarrow V^{*} given by the action of RR on II is the same as the natural map between those ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-modules. It is equivalent to require that RR have a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module basis ζ0=1,ζ1,…,ζn−1\zeta_{0}=1,\zeta_{1},\dots,\zeta_{n-1} and and II have a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module basis α1,α2,β1,…,βn−2\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{n-2} such that

the αi coefficient of ζj​βk is ​{1if i+j+k=n+1 0otherwise.\text{the $\alpha_{i}$ coefficient of $\zeta_{j}\beta_{k}$ is }\begin{cases}1&\text{if $i+j+k=n+1$ }\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

The equivalence can be computed by working out the natural map Symn−2⁡V∗⊗Symn−3⁡V→V∗\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}V^{*}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}V\rightarrow V^{*} in terms of an explicit basis. It is easy to see that when n=3n=3 this condition requires that II is isomorphic to RR as an RR-module. So we see here that only one of the ideal classes constructed is really new data, since the binary form, and thus all its associated ideal classes, can be recovered from RR, II, and the exact sequence above.

All of the work in the paper can be done with an arbitrary base scheme (or ring) replacing ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} in the above, and we now state a precise theorem capturing the above claims over an arbitrary base. Let SS be a scheme, and 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}} its sheaf of regular functions. A binary nn-ic form over SS is a locally free rank 22 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module VV, and an element f∈Symn⁡Vf\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V. An ll-twisted binary nn-ic form over SS is a locally free rank 22 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module VV, and an element f∈SymnV⊗(∧2V)⊗lf\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes l}. A binary nn-pair is an 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-algebra RR, an RR-module II, an exact sequence 0→Symn−3⁡Q∗→I→Q→00\rightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\rightarrow I\rightarrow Q\rightarrow 0 such that QQ is a locally free rank 22 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module, and an isomorphism R/𝒪S≅Symn−2⁡QR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\cong\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q that identifies the map R/𝒪S⊗Symn−3⁡Q∗→QR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\rightarrow Q induced from the action of RR on II with the natural map Symn−2⁡Q⊗Symn−3⁡Q∗→Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\rightarrow Q. In Section 3, we give a geometric construction of rings and modules from (twisted) binary nn-ic forms over a scheme SS, motivated by the geometric description given above over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. Our main theorem is the following, proved in Section 4.

Theorem 1.2.

For n≥3n\geq 3, we have a bijection between (−1)(-1)-twisted binary nn-ic forms over SS and binary nn-pairs over SS, and the bijection commutes with base change in S. In other words, we have a isomorphism of the moduli stack of (−1)(-1)-twisted binary nn-ic forms and the moduli stack of binary nn-pairs.

Analogs of Theorem 1.2 can be proven for ll-twisted binary forms for all ll. We have already given the idea of a geometric construction for one direction of the bijection in Theorem 1.2 (see Section 3 for the details), and we now give a simple construction of the other direction of the bijection. We can write the construction of a (−1)(-1)-twisted binary nn-ic form from a binary nn-pair as the evaluation

x↦x∧ϕ⁡(xn−2)​xx\mapsto x\wedge\phi(x^{n-2})x

of he above degree nn map Q→∧2QQ\rightarrow\wedge^{2}Q, where ϕ\phi is the isomorphism Symn−2⁡Q≅R/𝒪S\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\cong R/{\mathcal{O}_{S}} and we lift xx to the ideal II to act on it by RR and then take the quotient to QQ. It is not clear a priori that this map is even well-defined, but that will follow from the definition of a binary nn-pair (Lemma 4.5).

2 Constructing a ring and modules from a binary nn-ic form over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}

2.1 Concrete construction

In this section we will explicitly realize the ring and ideals associated to a binary nn-ic form inside a ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-algebra. Given a binary nn-ic form,

f0​xn+f1​xn−1​y+⋯+fn​ynwithfi∈ℤ,f_{0}x^{n}+f_{1}x^{n-1}y+\dots+f_{n}y^{n}\quad\textrm{with}\quad f_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}},

such that f0≠0f_{0}\neq 0, we can form a ring RfR_{f} as a subring of Qf:=ℚ⁡(θ)/(f0​θn+f1​θn−1+⋯+fn)Q_{f}:={\mathbb{Q}}(\theta)/(f_{0}\theta^{n}+f_{1}\theta^{n-1}+\dots+f_{n}) with ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module basis

(1) ζ0=1\displaystyle\zeta_{0}=1
ζ1=f0​θ\displaystyle\zeta_{1}=f_{0}\theta
ζ2=f0​θ2+f1​θ\displaystyle\zeta_{2}=f_{0}\theta^{2}+f_{1}\theta
ζk=f0​θk+⋯+fk−1​θ\displaystyle\zeta_{k}=f_{0}\theta^{k}+\dots+f_{k-1}\theta
ζn−1=f0​θn−1+⋯+fn−2​θ.\displaystyle\zeta_{n-1}=f_{0}\theta^{n-1}+\dots+f_{n-2}\theta.

Since f0≠0f_{0}\neq 0, we have that RfR_{f} is a free rank nn ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module, i.e. a rank nn ring in the terminology of Bhargava [2]. Birch and Merriman [3] studied this ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-submodule of QfQ_{f}, and Nakagawa [15, Proposition 1.1] proved that this ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-submodule is a ring (though Nakagawa worked only with irreducible ff, his proof makes sense for all ff). Nakagawa writes down the multiplication table of RfR_{f} explicitly as follows:

(2) ζiζj=−∑max⁡(i+j−n,1)≤k≤ifi+j−kζk+∑j<k≤min⁡(i+j,n)fi+j−kζkfor 1≤i,j≤n−1,\zeta_{i}\zeta_{j}=-\sum_{\max(i+j-n,1)\leq k\leq i}f_{i+j-k}\zeta_{k}+\sum_{j<k\leq\min(i+j,n)}f_{i+j-k}\zeta_{k}\quad\textrm{for }1\leq i,j\leq n-1,

where ζn:=−fn\zeta_{n}:=-f_{n}. If f0=0f_{0}=0, we could still use the above multiplication table to define a rank nn ring (see Section 2.2). We have the discriminant equality Disc⁡Rf=Disc⁡f\operatorname{Disc}R_{f}=\operatorname{Disc}f (see, for example, [17, Proposition 4]), which is a point of interest in RfR_{f} in previous works (e.g. [15], [17]).

Remark 2.1.

Throughout this paper, it will be useful to also make the above construction with ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} replaced by ℤ⁡[f0,…​fn]{\mathbb{Z}}[f_{0},\dots f_{n}], where the fif_{i} are formal variables, and with f=f0​xn+⋯+fn​ynf=f_{0}x^{n}+\dots+f_{n}y^{n}, which we call the universal form. If KK is the fraction field of ℤ⁡[f0,…​fn]{\mathbb{Z}}[f_{0},\dots f_{n}], we can then work in K⁡(θ)/(f0​θn+f1​θn−1+⋯+fn)K(\theta)/(f_{0}\theta^{n}+f_{1}\theta^{n-1}+\dots+f_{n}) instead of ℚ⁡(θ)/(f0​θn+f1​θn−1+⋯+fn){\mathbb{Q}}(\theta)/(f_{0}\theta^{n}+f_{1}\theta^{n-1}+\dots+f_{n}). The multiplication table in Equation (2) still holds, as Nakagawa’s proof can also be interpreted in this context.

When f0≠0f_{0}\neq 0, we can also form a fractional ideal If=(1,θ){I_{f}}=(1,\theta) of RfR_{f} (lying in QfQ_{f}). There is a natural GL2⁡(ℤ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}}) action on binary forms, and the ring RfR_{f} and the ideal class of If{I_{f}} are invariant under this action The invariance will follow from our geometric construction of this ideal in Section 2.3. (See also [15, Proposition 1.2] for a direct proof of the invariance of RfR_{f}, and [17, Théorème 3.4] which, in the case when ff is irreducible and primitive, considers a sequence of ideals 𝔍j\mathfrak{J}_{j}, all in the ideal class of If{I_{f}}, and proves that this ideal class is SL2\operatorname{SL}_{2} invariant.) The powers of If{I_{f}} give a sequence of ideals If0,If1,…,Ifn−1,…{I_{f}}^{0},{I_{f}}^{1},\dots,{I_{f}}^{n-1},\dots whose classes are each GL2⁡(ℤ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}}) invariant. We can write down the following explicit ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module bases for Ifk{I_{f}}^{k} for 0≤k≤n−10\leq k\leq n-1:

(3) Ifk=⟨1,θ,…,θk,ζk+1,…,ζn−1⟩ℤ,\displaystyle{I_{f}}^{k}=\langle 1,\theta,\dots,\theta^{k},\zeta_{k+1},\dots,\zeta_{n-1}\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}},

where ⟨s1,…,sn⟩R\langle s_{1},\dots,s_{n}\rangle_{R} denotes the RR-module generated by s1,…,sns_{1},\dots,s_{n}. Equivalently to Equation (3), we have for 0≤k≤n−10\leq k\leq n-1

(4) Ifk=⟨1,θ,…,θk,f0​θk+1,f0​θk+2+f1​θk+1,…,f0​θn−1+f1​θn−2+⋯+fn−k−2​θk+1⟩ℤ.{I_{f}}^{k}=\langle 1,\theta,\dots,\theta^{k},f_{0}\theta^{k+1},f_{0}\theta^{k+2}+f_{1}\theta^{k+1},\dots,f_{0}\theta^{n-1}+f_{1}\theta^{n-2}+\dots+f_{n-k-2}\theta^{k+1}\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}}.

To be clear, we give the boundary cases explicitly:

Ifn−2=⟨1,θ,…,θn−2,f0​θn−1⟩ℤ\displaystyle{I_{f}}^{n-2}=\langle 1,\theta,\dots,\theta^{n-2},f_{0}\theta^{n-1}\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}}
Ifn−1=⟨1,θ,…,θn−1⟩ℤ.\displaystyle{I_{f}}^{n-1}=\langle 1,\theta,\dots,\theta^{n-1}\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}}.

Proposition A.1 in the Appendix (Section A) shows that the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-modules given above are equal to the ideals we claim. Clearly, the given ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-modules are subsets of the respective ideals and contain the ideal generators, and so it only remains to check that the given ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-modules are actually ideals.

If we look at the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} bases of If2{I_{f}}^{2}, If1{I_{f}}^{1}, and If0{I_{f}}^{0} given in Equation (4), they naturally lead to considering another ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module (given by Equation (4) when k=−1k=-1)

(5) If#=⟨f0,f0​θ+f1,…,f0​θn−1+f1​θn−2+⋯+fn−1⟩ℤ.{I_{f}}^{\#}=\langle f_{0},f_{0}\theta+f_{1},\dots,f_{0}\theta^{n-1}+f_{1}\theta^{n-2}+\dots+f_{n-1}\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}}.

It turns out that If#{I_{f}}^{\#} is an ideal of RfR_{f}, which is shown in Proposition A.3 in the Appendix (Section A). This ideal is studied in the case of ff irreducible and primitive as 𝔟\mathfrak{b} in [17] and [19] and as 𝔅\mathfrak{B} in [6].

Remark 2.2.

Similarly, we can form the fractional ideals IfkI_{f}^{k} and If#I_{f}^{\#} over the base ring ℤ⁡[f0,…​fn]{\mathbb{Z}}[f_{0},\dots f_{n}] and with f=f0​xn++⋯+fn​ynf=f_{0}x^{n}++\dots+f_{n}y^{n}, working in K⁡(θ)/(f0​θn+f1​θn−1+⋯+fn)K(\theta)/(f_{0}\theta^{n}+f_{1}\theta^{n-1}+\dots+f_{n}). The ideals have ℤ⁡[f0,…​fn]{\mathbb{Z}}[f_{0},\dots f_{n}]-module bases as given in Equations (3), (4), and (5), and these ℤ⁡[f0,…​fn]{\mathbb{Z}}[f_{0},\dots f_{n}]-modules are RR ideals by the same proofs as in the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} case.

Given the sequence If2,If1,If0{I_{f}}^{2},{I_{f}}^{1},{I_{f}}^{0} that led us to define If#{I_{f}}^{\#} one might expect that If#{I_{f}}^{\#} is the same as If−1{I_{f}}^{-1}. However, it turns out that If{I_{f}} is not always invertible. We do have the following proposition (proven in Proposition A.4 of the Appendix (Section A)). A form ff is primitive if its coefficients generate the unit ideal in ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}.

Proposition 2.3.

For f≢0f\not\equiv 0, the ideal class of If{I_{f}} is invertible if and only if the form ff is primitive. Also, the ideal class of If#{I_{f}}^{\#} is invertible if and only if the form ff is primitive. In the case that ff is primitive, If−1=If#{I_{f}}^{-1}={I_{f}}^{\#}.

When ff is primitive, Simon [18, Proposition 3.2] proved that the ideal classes of what we call If{I_{f}} and If#{I_{f}}^{\#} are inverses. Of course, for any k>0k>0, we have Ifk{I_{f}}^{k} is invertible if and only if If{I_{f}} is. Some of the ideal classes Ifk{I_{f}}^{k} are particularly interesting. For example, we have the following result which we prove in Corollary 3.7.

Theorem 2.4.

The class of Ifn−2{I_{f}}^{n-2} is the class of the inverse different of RfR_{f}. In other words, as RfR_{f} modules, Ifn−2≅Homℤ⁡(Rf,ℤ){I_{f}}^{n-2}\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(R_{f},{\mathbb{Z}}).

Simon [19, Proposition 14] independently discovered that when ff is primitive and irreducible that (If#)2−n({I_{f}}^{\#})^{2-n} is in the ideal class of the inverse different of RfR_{f}. In this paper, we find that while (If#)2−n({I_{f}}^{\#})^{2-n} is not naturally constructed as a module, Ifn−2{I_{f}}^{n-2} can be naturally constructed and is always the inverse different, even when ff is reducible, primitive, or the zero form! When f≡0f\equiv 0, we construct Ifn−2{I_{f}}^{n-2} as a module and the above theorem holds, but the module is not realizable as a fractional ideal of RfR_{f}.

Corollary 2.5.

For n≠2n\neq 2 and f≢0f\not\equiv 0, the ring RfR_{f} is Gorenstein if and only if the form ff is primitive.

Proof.

It is known that for rank nn rings, the condition of Gorenstein is equivalent to the inverse different being invertible. For the ring RfR_{f}, the inverse different is in the same ideal class as Ifn−2{I_{f}}^{n-2} and thus this follows from Proposition 2.3. ∎

Remark 2.6.

When we have a binary form with f0=±1f_{0}=\pm 1, then Rf=ℤ⁡[θ]/f⁡(θ)R_{f}={\mathbb{Z}}[\theta]/f(\theta). Such rings, generated by one element, are called monogenic. We see that all monogenic rings are RfR_{f} for some binary form ff. Also, in this case Ifk≅If#≅Rf{I_{f}}^{k}\cong I_{f}^{\#}\cong R_{f} as RfR_{f}-modules.

2.2 Explicit multiplication and action tables

If a form f=f0​xn+f1​xn−1​y+⋯+fn​ynf=f_{0}x^{n}+f_{1}x^{n-1}y+\dots+f_{n}y^{n} has f0=0f_{0}=0, but f≢0f\not\equiv 0, then we can act by GL2⁡(ℤ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}}) to take ff to a form f′f^{\prime} with f0′≠0f_{0}^{\prime}\neq 0. We then can define the ring RfR_{f} and the RfR_{f} ideal classes If{I_{f}} and If#{I_{f}}^{\#} using f′f^{\prime}. Since the ring and ideal classes are GL2⁡(ℤ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}}) invariants, it does not matter which f′f^{\prime} we use. In this section, we give a more systematic way to define the rings RfR_{f} and ideal classes If{I_{f}} that works even when f≡0f\equiv 0.

Given a base ring BB, if we form a rank nn BB-module R=B​r1⊕…​B​rnR=Br_{1}\oplus\dots Br_{n}, we can specify a BB-bilinear product on RR by letting

ri​rj=∑k=1nci,j,k​rkfor ​ci,j,k∈B,r_{i}r_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}c_{i,j,k}r_{k}\quad\textrm{for }c_{i,j,k}\in B,

and e=∑k=1nek​rke=\sum_{k=1}^{n}e_{k}r_{k} for some ek∈Be_{k}\in B. If this product is commutative, associative, and ee is a multiplicative identity (which is a queston of certain polynomial equalities with integer coefficients being satisfied by the ci,j,kc_{i,j,k} and eke_{k}) then we call the ci,j,kc_{i,j,k} and eke_{k} a multiplication table. A multiplication table gives a ring RR with a specified BB-module basis.

Similarly, we can form a free rank mm BB-module I=B​α1⊕…​B​αmI=B\alpha_{1}\oplus\dots B\alpha_{m}, where usually mm is a multiple of nn. Then we can specify a BB-bilinear product R×I→BR\times I\rightarrow B by

ri​αj=∑k=1mdi,j,k​αkfor ​di,j,k∈B.r_{i}\alpha_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{m}d_{i,j,k}\alpha_{k}\quad\textrm{for }d_{i,j,k}\in B.

That this product gives an RR-module action on II is a question of certain polynomial equalities with integer coefficients being satisfied by the di,j,kd_{i,j,k}, ci,j,kc_{i,j,k} and eke_{k}, and in the case they are satisfied we call the di,j,kd_{i,j,k} an action table. An action table gives an RR-module II with a specified BB-module basis.

If we want to work directly with forms with f0=0f_{0}=0 (for example, to deal with the form f≡0f\equiv 0 or to study the form f=x2​y+x​y2f=x^{2}y+xy^{2} when we replace ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} with ℤ/2​ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}/2{\mathbb{Z}}), we see that we can define a ring ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} from the multiplication table given in Equation (2). The conditions of commutativity and associativity on this multiplication table are polynomial identities in the fif_{i} since the construction of RR can also be made with the universal form.

Equations (3) and (5) display ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module bases of If{I_{f}} and If#{I_{f}}^{\#}. The action of elements of RfR_{f} on these ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module bases is given by an action table of polynomials in the fif_{i} with ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} coefficients. (We can see this, for example, because the proofs of Propositions A.1 and A.3 work over the base ring ℤ⁡[f0,…,fn]{\mathbb{Z}}[f_{0},\dots,f_{n}].) These polynomials in the fif_{i} formally give an action table because they give an action table over the base ring ℤ⁡[f0,…,fn]{\mathbb{Z}}[f_{0},\dots,f_{n}]. Thus, we can construct ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-modules ℐf{\mathcal{I}_{f}} and ℐf#{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\#} first as rank nn ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-modules and then give them an ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} action by the same polynomials in the fif_{i} that make the action tables for If{I_{f}} and If#{I_{f}}^{\#} respectively.

We can also form versions of the powers of If{I_{f}} this way, which are ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-modules that we call ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} for 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1. We use the action table of Ifk{I_{f}}^{k} with the basis of Equation (3). The action table has entries that are integer polynomials in the fif_{i} for the same reasons as above. We only have defined the ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} as ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-modules and not as fractional ideals of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}. Whenever f≢0f\not\equiv 0, however, we have also given a a realization of the ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} as the ideal class IfkI_{f}^{k} (or If#I_{f}^{\#} when k=−1k=-1). Let ℐf−1:=ℐf#{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{-1}:={\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\#} and ℐf:=ℐf1{\mathcal{I}_{f}}:={\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{1}. We do not put the kk in the exponent because even when ff is non-zero but non-primitive, it is not clear that the module ℐfk{{\mathcal{I}_{f}}}_{k} is a power of the module ℐf{\mathcal{I}_{f}}. When ff is primitive, since IfI_{f} is invertible, its ideal class powers are the same as its module powers.

2.3 Simple geometric construction

For many reasons, we desire a canonical, basis free description of the ring ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} and ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-modules ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}. We would like to deal more uniformly with the case that f0=0f_{0}=0 and see easily the GL2⁡(ℤ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}}) invariance of our constructions. A binary nn-ic form ff describes a subscheme of ℙℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}} which we call Sf{S_{f}}. Let 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k) denote the usual sheaf on ℙℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}} and let 𝒪Sf​(k)\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k) denote its pullback to Sf{S_{f}}. Also, for a sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F}, let Γ⁡(U,ℱ)\Gamma(U,\mathcal{F}) be sections of ℱ\mathcal{F} on UU and let Γ⁡(ℱ)\Gamma(\mathcal{F}) be the global sections of ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Theorem 2.7.

For a binary form f≢0f\not\equiv 0, the ring Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}) of global functions of Sf{S_{f}} is isomorphic to RfR_{f}. The global sections Γ​(𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}(k)) have an Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}})-module structure, and since Rf≅Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)R_{f}\cong\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}), this gives Γ​(𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}(k)) an RfR_{f}-module structure. For, 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1, the global sections Γ​(𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}(k)) are isomorphic to Ifk{I_{f}}^{k} as an RfR_{f}-module. The global sections Γ​(𝒪Sf​(−1))\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}(-1)) are isomorphic to If#{I_{f}}^{\#} as an RfR_{f}-module.

Proof.

We can act by GL2⁡(ℤ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}}) so that f0≠0f_{0}\neq 0 and fn≠0f_{n}\neq 0. Then if we write ℙℤ1=Proj⁡ℤ⁡[x,y]{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}}=\operatorname{Proj}{\mathbb{Z}}[x,y], we can cover ℙℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}} with the open subsets UyU_{y} and UxU_{x} where yy and xx are invertible, respectively.

Lemma 2.8.

If fn≠0f_{n}\neq 0, then the restriction map

Γ⁡(Uy,𝒪Sf​(k))\displaystyle\Gamma(U_{y},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)) →Γ⁡(Uy∩Ux,𝒪Sf​(k))\displaystyle\rightarrow\Gamma(U_{y}\cap U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k))

is injective.

Proof.

If ∑i≥−kai​xk+i​y−i↦0\sum_{i\geq-k}a_{i}x^{k+i}y^{-i}\mapsto 0, with ai∈ℤa_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}}, then ∑i≥−kai​xk+i​y−i=∑jdj​xj​yk−n−j​f\sum_{i\geq-k}a_{i}x^{k+i}y^{-i}=\sum_{j}d_{j}x^{j}y^{k-n-j}f, where dj∈ℤd_{j}\in{\mathbb{Z}}. Since ∑i≥−kai​xk+i​y−i\sum_{i\geq-k}a_{i}x^{k+i}y^{-i} has no terms of negative degree in xx and fn≠0f_{n}\neq 0, we conclude that dj=0d_{j}=0 for j<0.j<0. Thus, ∑i≥−kai​xk+i​y−i\sum_{i\geq-k}a_{i}x^{k+i}y^{-i} is 0 in Γ⁡(Uy,𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(U_{y},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)). ∎

Similarly, since f0≠0f_{0}\neq 0, we have that Γ⁡(Ux,𝒪Sf​(k))→Γ⁡(Uy∩Ux,𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k))\rightarrow\Gamma(U_{y}\cap U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)) is an injection.

So we wish to determine the elements of Γ⁡(Uy∩Ux,𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(U_{y}\cap U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)) that are in the images of both Γ⁡(Ux,𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)) and Γ⁡(Uy,𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(U_{y},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)) First, note that xk,xk−1​y,…,ykx^{k},x^{k-1}y,\dots,y^{k} are in the images of both restriction maps. In Γ⁡(Uy∩Ux,𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(U_{y}\cap U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)) for 1≤m≤n−k−11\leq m\leq n-k-1, we have

f0​xk+m​y−m+⋯+fk+m−1​x​yk−1=−fk+m​yk−⋯−fn​xk+m−n​yn−m,f_{0}x^{k+m}y^{-m}+\dots+f_{k+m-1}xy^{k-1}=-f_{k+m}y^{k}-\dots-f_{n}x^{k+m-n}y^{n-m},

and thus zm:=f0​xk+m​y−m+…​fk+m−1​x​yk−1z_{m}:=f_{0}x^{k+m}y^{-m}+\dots f_{k+m-1}xy^{k-1} is in the images of both Γ⁡(Ux,𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)) and Γ⁡(Uy,𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(U_{y},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)).

Now, let pp be in both images so that p=∑i≥−kai​xk+i​y−i=∑i≤−kbi​x−i​yk+ip=\sum_{i\geq-k}a_{i}x^{k+i}y^{-i}=\sum_{i\leq-k}b_{i}x^{-i}y^{k+i} with ai,bi∈ℤa_{i},b_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}}. If a=∑i≥−kai​xk+i​y−i∈Γ⁡(Uy,𝒪Sf​(k))a=\sum_{i\geq-k}a_{i}x^{k+i}y^{-i}\in\Gamma(U_{y},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)) and b=∑i≤0bi​x−i​yk+i∈Γ⁡(Ux,𝒪Sf​(k))b=\sum_{i\leq 0}b_{i}x^{-i}y^{k+i}\in\Gamma(U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)), then we have a formal equality a−b=∑ici​xi​yk−i−n​fa-b=\sum_{i}c_{i}x^{i}y^{k-i-n}f (in ℤ⁡[x,x−1,y,y−1]{\mathbb{Z}}[x,x^{-1},y,y^{-1}]) where ci∈ℤc_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}}. We can assume without loss of generality that ci=0c_{i}=0 for i≥0i\geq 0 because any ci​xi​yk−i−n​fc_{i}x^{i}y^{k-i-n}f with ii non-negative we could just subtract from the representation aa to obtain another such representation of pp in Γ⁡(Uy,𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(U_{y},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)). Similarly, we can assume that ci=0c_{i}=0 for i≤k−ni\leq k-n. From the equality a−b=∑i=−n+k+1−1xi​yk−i−n​fa-b=\sum_{i=-n+k+1}^{-1}x^{i}y^{k-i-n}f, we can conclude that aa is a linear combination of xk,xk−1​y,…,ykx^{k},x^{k-1}y,\dots,y^{k} plus all the terms ∑i=−n+k+1−1xi​yk−i−n​f\sum_{i=-n+k+1}^{-1}x^{i}y^{k-i-n}f of positive degree in xx, and bb is that same linear combination minus all the terms of ∑i=−n+k+1−1xi​yk−i−n​f\sum_{i=-n+k+1}^{-1}x^{i}y^{k-i-n}f of positive degree in xx. The terms of positive degree in xx of xi​yk−i−n​fx^{i}y^{k-i-n}f sum to zn+i−kz_{n+i-k}. Thus, a∈⟨xk,xk−1​y,…,yk,z1,…,zn−1−k⟩ℤa\in\left\langle x^{k},x^{k-1}y,\dots,y^{k},z_{1},\dots,z_{n-1-k}\right\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}}.

For k≥0k\geq 0, when we map ⟨xk,xk−1​y,…,yk,z1,…,zn−1−k⟩ℤ\left\langle x^{k},x^{k-1}y,\dots,y^{k},z_{1},\dots,z_{n-1-k}\right\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}} to QfQ_{f} via x↦θx\mapsto\theta and y↦1y\mapsto 1, the image is the free rank nn ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module ⟨1,θ,…,θk,ζk+1,…,ζn−1⟩ℤ\left\langle 1,\theta,\dots,\theta^{k},\zeta_{k+1},\dots,\zeta_{n-1}\right\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}}. Thus, the map is an isomorphism of ⟨xk,xk−1​y,…,yk,z1,…,zn−1−k⟩ℤ\left\langle x^{k},x^{k-1}y,\dots,y^{k},z_{1},\dots,z_{n-1-k}\right\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}}, the global sections of 𝒪Sf​(k)\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k), onto Ifk{I_{f}}^{k}. Clearly the Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}})-module structure on Γ​(𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)) is the same as the the RfR_{f}-module structure on Ifk{I_{f}}^{k} (including the k=0k=0 case, which gives the ring isomorphism Rf≅Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)R_{f}\cong\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}})). When k=−1k=-1, when we map ⟨z1,…,zn⟩ℤ\left\langle z_{1},\dots,z_{n}\right\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}} to QfQ_{f} via x↦θx\mapsto\theta and y↦1y\mapsto 1, the image is the free rank nn ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module If#{I_{f}}^{\#}. Similarly we conclude the theorem for If#{I_{f}}^{\#}. ∎

Note that though 𝒪Sf​(k)\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k) is always an invertible 𝒪Sf\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}-module, when Sf{S_{f}} is not affine, the global sections Γ​(𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}(k)) are not necessarily an invertible Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}})-module. In fact, we know that for nonzero ff and 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1 that Γ​(𝒪Sf​(k))\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k)) is an invertible Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}})-module exactly when ff is primitive.

Theorem 2.9.

Let ff be a binary form with non-zero discriminant. The scheme Sf{S_{f}} is affine if and only if ff is primitive.

Proof.

From Theorem 2.7 we see that if Sf{S_{f}} is affine, then since Γ⁡(𝒪Sf​(1))≅If\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}(1))\cong{I_{f}} and 𝒪Sf​(1)\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}(1) is invertible we must have that If{I_{f}} is an invertible RfR_{f}-module. Thus by Proposition 2.3, if Sf{S_{f}} is affine then ff is primitive. We see that Sf{S_{f}} has a vertical fiber over (p)(p) when p|fp\mid f. Moreover, when p|fp\mid f we see from the multiplication table (Equation (2)) that the fiber of aa over (p)(p) is the non-reduced nn-dimensional point Spec⁡ℤ/(p)​[x1,x2,…,xn−1]/(xi​xj)1≤i,j≤n−1\operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb{Z}}_{/(p)}[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n-1}]/(x_{i}x_{j})_{1\leq i,j\leq n-1} which does not embed into ℙℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}}.

Now suppose that ff is primitive and has non-zero discriminant. We can change variables so that f0≠0f_{0}\neq 0 and fn≠0f_{n}\neq 0. From the standard open affine cover of ℙℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}}, we have that Sf{S_{f}} is covered by affine opens Uy=Spec⁡ℤ⁡[x/y]/(f/yn)U_{y}=\operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb{Z}}[x/y]/(f/y^{n}) and Ux=Spec⁡ℤ⁡[y/x]/(f/xn)U_{x}=\operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb{Z}}[y/x]/(f/x^{n}). Since RfR_{f} is a finitely generated ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module inside QfQ_{f} (which is a product of number fields), we know that the class group of RfR_{f} is finite. So, let mm be such that (If#)m({I_{f}}^{\#})^{m} is principal. (Note that by Proposition A.4 we know that (If#)({I_{f}}^{\#}) is an invertible RfR_{f}-module.) Let J=θ​If#J=\theta{I_{f}}^{\#} which is an integral RfR_{f}-ideal. Let Jm=(b)J^{m}=(b) and (If#)m=(a)({I_{f}}^{\#})^{m}=(a), with a,b∈Rfa,b\in R_{f}. As in the computation in the proof of Proposition A.4, we see that If#+J=(1){I_{f}}^{\#}+J=(1) and thus there exists α,β∈Rf\alpha,\beta\in R_{f} such that α​a+β​b=1\alpha a+\beta b=1. We claim that (Sf)a=Uy({S_{f}})_{a}=U_{y} as open subschemes of Sf{S_{f}}, where (Sf)a({S_{f}})_{a} denotes the points of Sf{S_{f}} at which aa is non-zero.

In the ring QfQ_{f} we have that a​θm=b​ua\theta^{m}=bu, where uu is a unit in RfR_{f}. In Γ⁡(Uy∩Ux,𝒪Sf)≅Qf\Gamma(U_{y}\cap U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}})\cong Q_{f} this translates to a​(xy)m=b​ua(\frac{x}{y})^{m}=bu Thus

a⁡(α+βu​(xy)m)=α​a+β​au​(xy)m=α​a+β​b=1a(\alpha+\frac{\beta}{u}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^{m})=\alpha a+\beta\frac{a}{u}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^{m}=\alpha a+\beta b=1

in Γ⁡(Uy,𝒪Sf)\Gamma(U_{y},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}) (which injects into Γ⁡(Uy∩Ux,𝒪Sf)≅Qf\Gamma(U_{y}\cap U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}})\cong Q_{f}). Therefore aa is not zero at any point of UyU_{y}, and so Uy⊂(Sf)aU_{y}\subset({S_{f}})_{a}. Suppose that we have a point p∉Uyp\not\in U_{y} so that yx\frac{y}{x} is 0 at pp. Since in Γ⁡(Uy∩Ux,𝒪Sf)\Gamma(U_{y}\cap U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}) we have a=b​u​(yx)ma=bu(\frac{y}{x})^{m}, this is also true in Γ⁡(Ux,𝒪Sf)≅ℤ⁡[y/x]/F⁡(y/x)\Gamma(U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}})\cong{\mathbb{Z}}[y/x]/F(y/x) (which injects into Γ⁡(Uy∩Ux,𝒪Sf)\Gamma(U_{y}\cap U_{x},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}})). Since we have p∈Uxp\in U_{x}, then aa is also 0 at pp and so p∉(Sf)ap\not\in({S_{f}})_{a} and we conclude (Sf)a⊂Uy({S_{f}})_{a}\subset U_{y}. We have shown (Sf)a=Uy({S_{f}})_{a}=U_{y} and by switching xx and yy we see similarly that (Sf)b=Ux({S_{f}})_{b}=U_{x}. Since (a,b)(a,b) is the unit ideal in Γ⁡(Sf,𝒪Sf)≅Rf\Gamma({S_{f}},\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}})\cong R_{f}, and (Sf)a({S_{f}})_{a} and (Sf)b({S_{f}})_{b} are each affine, we have that Sf{S_{f}} is affine ([12, Exercise 2.17(b)]).

We could similarly argue over a localization of ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}, and thus localizing away from the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} primes that divide ff, the scheme Sf{S_{f}} is the same as Spec⁡Rf\operatorname{Spec}R_{f}. Over the primes of ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} that divide ff, SfS_{f} has vertical fibers isomorphic to ℙℤ/p​ℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{{\mathbb{Z}}/p{\mathbb{Z}}} but Spec⁡Rf\operatorname{Spec}R_{f} has a non-reduced nn-dimensional point. ∎

2.4 Geometric construction by hypercohomology

The description of RfR_{f} as the global functions of the subscheme given by ff is very satisfying as a coordinate-free, canonical and simple description of RfR_{f}, but still does not take care of the form f≡0f\equiv 0. It may seem at first that f≡0f\equiv 0 is a pesky, uninteresting case, but we will eventually want to reduce a form so that its coefficients are in ℤ/p​ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}/p{\mathbb{Z}}, in which case many of our non-zero forms will go to 0. In general we may want to base change, and the formation of the ring Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}) does not commute with base change. For example, a non-zero binary nn-ic all of whose coefficients are divisible pp will give a rank nn ring Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}) but the reduction f¯\bar{f} of ff to ℤ/p​ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}/p{\mathbb{Z}} would give Sf¯=ℙℤ/p​ℤ1S_{\bar{f}}={\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{{\mathbb{Z}}/p{\mathbb{Z}}} and thus a ring of global functions that is rank 1 over ℤ/p​ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}/p{\mathbb{Z}}.

We can, however, make the following construction, which was given for n=3n=3 by Deligne in a letter [7] to Gan, Gross, and Savin. On ℙℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}} a binary nn-ic form ff gives 𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}, whose image is the ideal sheaf of Sf{S_{f}}. We can consider 𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O} as a complex in degrees -1 and 0, and then take the hypercohomology of this complex:

(6) R=H0​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪).R=H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}\right).

(Here we are taking the 0th right hyper-derived functor of the pushforward by π:ℙℤ1→Spec⁡ℤ\pi:{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}}\rightarrow\operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb{Z}} on this complex. Alternatively, we pushforward the complex in the derived category and then take H0H^{0}. We take hypercohomology since we are applying the functor to a complex of sheaves and not just a single sheaf.) There is a product on the complex 𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O} given as 𝒪⊗𝒪→𝒪\mathcal{O}\otimes\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathcal{O} by multiplication, 𝒪⊗𝒪⁡(−n)→𝒪⁡(−n)\mathcal{O}\otimes\mathcal{O}(-n)\rightarrow\mathcal{O}(-n) by the 𝒪\mathcal{O}-module action, and 𝒪⁡(−n)⊗𝒪⁡(−n)→0\mathcal{O}(-n)\otimes\mathcal{O}(-n)\rightarrow 0. This product is clearly commutative and associative, and induces a product on RR. The map of complexes

𝒪↓𝒪⁡(−n)→𝒪\begin{CD}\mathcal{O}\\ @V{}V{}V\\ \mathcal{O}(-n)@>{}>{}>\mathcal{O}\end{CD}

induces ℤ→R{\mathbb{Z}}\rightarrow R. (Of course, H0​R​π∗​(𝒪)H^{0}R\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O}) is just π∗​(𝒪)≅ℤ\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O})\cong{\mathbb{Z}}.) It is easy to see that 1∈H0​R​π∗​(𝒪)1\in H^{0}R\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O}) acts as the multiplicative identity.

When f≢0f\not\equiv 0, the map 𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O} is injective, and thus the complex 𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O} is homotopy equivalent to 𝒪/f⁡(𝒪⁡(−n))≅𝒪Sf\mathcal{O}/f(\mathcal{O}(-n))\cong\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}} (as a chain complex in the 0th degree). The homotopy equivalence also respects the product structure on the complexes. Thus when f≢0f\not\equiv 0, we have R≅π∗​(𝒪Sf)R\cong\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}), and since Spec⁡ℤ\operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb{Z}} is affine we can consider π∗​(𝒪Sf)\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}}) simply as a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module isomorphic to Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)≅Rf\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{{S_{f}}})\cong R_{f}. When f≡0f\equiv 0 we have

R=H0​R​π∗​(𝒪)⊕H1​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n))≅ℤ⊕ℤn−1R=H^{0}R\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O})\oplus H^{1}R\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O}(-n))\cong{\mathbb{Z}}\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-1}

as a ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-module and with multiplication given by (1,0)(1,0) acting as the multiplicative identity and (0,x)​(0,y)=0(0,x)(0,y)=0 for all x,y∈ℤn−1x,y\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-1}. This agrees with the definition of ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} given in Section 2.2 that used the coefficients of ff to give a multiplication table for ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}. So we see this definition of RR is a natural extension to all ff of the construction Γ⁡(𝒪Sf)\Gamma(\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}) for non-zero ff, especially since RR gives a rank nn ring even when f≡0f\equiv 0.

Theorem 2.10.

For all binary nn-ic forms ff, we have

ℛf≅H0​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪){\mathcal{R}_{f}}\cong H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}\right)

as rings. (Note that ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} is defined in Section 2.2.)

Proof.

The proof of Theorem 2.7 shows that ℛf≅H0​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪){\mathcal{R}_{f}}\cong H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}\right) for the universal form f=f0​xn+f1​xn−1​y+⋯+fn​ynf=f_{0}x^{n}+f_{1}x^{n-1}y+\dots+f_{n}y^{n} with coefficients in ℤ⁡[f0,…,fn]{\mathbb{Z}}[f_{0},\dots,f_{n}]. Since both the construction of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} from the multiplication table in Section 2.2 and the formation of H0​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪)H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}\right) commute with base change (as we will see in Theorem 3.2), and every form ff is a base change of the universal form, the theorem follows. ∎

We have a similar description of the ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} ideal classes (or modules) ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}. We can define ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-modules for all k∈ℤk\in{\mathbb{Z}}:

H0​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n+k)→f𝒪⁡(k)).H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(k)\right).

(Here, 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k) is in degree 0 in the above complex.) The ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-module structure on

H0​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n+k)→f𝒪⁡(k))H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(k)\right)

is given by the following action of the complex 𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O} on the complex 𝒪⁡(−n+k)→f𝒪⁡(k):\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(k):

𝒪⊗𝒪⁡(k)→𝒪⁡(k)𝒪⊗𝒪⁡(−n+k)→𝒪⁡(−n+k)\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\otimes\mathcal{O}(k)\rightarrow\mathcal{O}(k)\qquad\mathcal{O}\otimes\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\rightarrow\mathcal{O}(-n+k)
𝒪⁡(−n)⊗𝒪⁡(k)→𝒪⁡(−n+k)𝒪⁡(−n)⊗𝒪⁡(−n+k)→0,\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(-n)\otimes\mathcal{O}(k)\rightarrow\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\qquad\mathcal{O}(-n)\otimes\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\rightarrow 0,

where all maps are the natural ones.

Theorem 2.11.

For all binary nn-ic forms ff and −1≤k≤n−1-1\leq k\leq n-1 we have

ℐfk≅H0​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n+k)→f𝒪⁡(k)){\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}\cong H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(k)\right)

as ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-modules.

Proof.

The proof is that same as that of Theorem 2.10. ∎

We have the following nice corollary of Theorems 2.10 and 2.11.

Corollary 2.12.

The ring ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} and the ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-module ℐf{\mathcal{I}_{f}} are GL2⁡(ℤ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}}) invariants of binary nn-ic forms ff.

3 Constructing rings and modules from a binary form over an arbitrary base

So far, we have mainly considered binary forms with coefficients in ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. We will now develop our theory over an arbitrary base scheme SS. When S=Spec⁡BS=\operatorname{Spec}B we will sometimes say we are working over a base ring BB and we will replace 𝒪S\mathcal{O}_{S}-modules with their corresponding BB-modules.

Notation. For an 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module MM, we write M∗M^{*} to denote the 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}} dual ℋ​o​m𝒪S​(M,𝒪S)\mathcal{H}om_{\mathcal{O}_{S}}(M,{\mathcal{O}_{S}}). If ℱ\mathcal{F} is a sheaf, we use s∈ℱs\in\mathcal{F} to denote that ss is a global section of ℱ\mathcal{F}. We use Symn⁡M\operatorname{Sym}^{n}M to denote the usual quotient of M⊗nM^{\otimes n}, and Symn⁡M\operatorname{Sym}_{n}M to denote the submodule of symmetric elements of M⊗nM^{\otimes n}. We have (Symn⁡M)∗≅Symn⁡M∗(\operatorname{Sym}_{n}M)^{*}\cong\operatorname{Sym}^{n}M^{*} for locally free 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-modules MM.

A binary nn-ic form over SS is a pair (f,V)(f,V) where VV is a locally free 𝒪S\mathcal{O}_{S}-module of rank 2 and f∈Symn⁡Vf\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V. An isomorphism of binary nn-ic forms (f,V)(f,V) and (f,V′)(f,V^{\prime}) is given by an 𝒪S\mathcal{O}_{S}-module isomorphism V≅V′V\cong V^{\prime} which takes ff to f′f^{\prime}. We call ff a binary form when nn is clear from context or not relevant. If VV is the free 𝒪S\mathcal{O}_{S}-module 𝒪S​x⊕𝒪S​y\mathcal{O}_{S}x\oplus\mathcal{O}_{S}y we call ff a free binary form.

Given a binary form f∈Symn⁡Vf\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V over a base scheme SS, the form ff determines a subscheme Sf{S_{f}} of ℙ⁡(V){\mathbb{P}}(V) (where we define ℙ⁡(V)=Proj⁡Sym∗⁡V{\mathbb{P}}(V)=\operatorname{Proj}\operatorname{Sym}^{*}V). Let π:ℙ⁡(V)→S\pi:{\mathbb{P}}(V)\rightarrow S. Let 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k) denote the usual sheaf on ℙ⁡(V){\mathbb{P}}(V) and 𝒪Sf​(k)\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k) denote the pullback of 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k) to Sf{S_{f}}. Then we can define the 𝒪S\mathcal{O}_{S}-algebra

(7) ℛf:=H0​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪),{\mathcal{R}_{f}}:=H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}\right),

where 𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O} is a complex in degrees -1 and 0. (In section 2.4 this point of view is worked out in detail over S=Spec⁡ℤS=\operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb{Z}}.) The product of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} is given by the natural product of the complex 𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O} with itself and the 𝒪S\mathcal{O}_{S}-algebra structure is induced from the map of 𝒪\mathcal{O} as a complex in degree 0 to the complex 𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}.

When 𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O} is injective, we have

ℛf=π∗​(𝒪Sf),{\mathcal{R}_{f}}=\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}),

as in Section 2.4. Similarly, we can define an ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-module

(8) ℐfk:=H0​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n+k)→f𝒪⁡(k)),{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}:=H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(k)\right),

for all k∈ℤk\in{\mathbb{Z}}. Let ℐf#:=ℐf−1{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\#}:={\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{-1} and ℐf:=ℐf1{\mathcal{I}_{f}}:={\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{1}. Clearly ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} and ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} are invariant under the GL⁡(V)\operatorname{GL}(V) action on forms in Symn⁡V\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V. Again, when 𝒪⁡(−n+k)→f𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(k) is injective, we have

ℐfk=π∗​(𝒪Sf​(k)){\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}=\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k))

for all k∈ℤk\in{\mathbb{Z}}.

Example 3.1.

If B=ℤ⊕ℤB={\mathbb{Z}}\oplus{\mathbb{Z}} and (fi)=ℤ⊕{0}(f_{i})={\mathbb{Z}}\oplus\{0\}, then in ℙℤ⊕ℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{{\mathbb{Z}}\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}} over the first Spec⁡ℤ\operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb{Z}} the form ff cuts out Spec⁡Rp⁡(f)\operatorname{Spec}R_{p(f)}, where p⁡(f)p(f) is the projection of ff onto the first factor of (ℤ⊕ℤ)​[x,y]({\mathbb{Z}}\oplus{\mathbb{Z}})[x,y]. Over the second copy of Spec⁡ℤ\operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb{Z}}, the form ff is 0 and cuts out all of ℙℤ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbb{Z}}. Here 𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O} is not injective because ff is a 0 divisor. Thus the ring ℛf:=H0​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪){\mathcal{R}_{f}}:=H^{0}R\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}) is not just the global functions of Sf{S_{f}} but also has a contribution from ker⁡(𝒪⁡(−n)→f𝒪)\ker(\mathcal{O}(-n)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}).

Unlike pushing forward 𝒪Sf​(k)\mathcal{O}_{S_{f}}(k) to SS, the constructions of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} and ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} for −1≤k≤n−1-1\leq k\leq n-1 commutes with base change.

Theorem 3.2.

Let f∈Symn⁡Vf\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V be a binary form over a base scheme SS. The construction of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} and ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} for −1≤k≤n−1-1\leq k\leq n-1 commutes with base change. More precisely, let ϕ:T→S\phi:T\rightarrow S be a map of schemes. Let ϕ∗​f∈Symn⁡ϕ∗​V\phi^{*}f\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}\phi^{*}V be the pullback of ff. Then the natural map from cohomology

ℛf⊗𝒪T→ℛϕ∗​f{\mathcal{R}_{f}}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{T}\rightarrow{\mathcal{R}_{\phi^{*}f}}

is an isomorphism of 𝒪T\mathcal{O}_{T}-algebras. Also, for −1≤k≤n−1-1\leq k\leq n-1, the natural map from cohomology

ℐf⊗𝒪T→ℐϕ∗​f{\mathcal{I}_{f}}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{T}\rightarrow{\mathcal{I}_{\phi^{*}f}}

is an isomorphism of ℛϕ∗​f{\mathcal{R}_{\phi^{*}f}}-modules (where the ℛϕ∗​f{\mathcal{R}_{\phi^{*}f}}-module structure on ℐf⊗𝒪T{\mathcal{I}_{f}}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{T} comes from the (ℛf⊗𝒪T)({\mathcal{R}_{f}}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{T})-module structure.

Proof.

The key to this proof is to compute all cohomology of the pushforward of the complex 𝒞⁡(k):𝒪⁡(−n+k)→f𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{C}(k):\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(k). This can be done using the long exact sequence of cohomology from the short exact sequence of complexes given in Equation (12) in the next section. In particular, 𝒞⁡(k)\mathcal{C}(k) does not have any cohomology in degrees other than 0. Since k≤n−1k\leq n-1, we have that H0​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(−n+k))=0H^{0}R\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O}(-n+k))=0 and thus H−1​R​π∗​(𝒞⁡(k))=0H^{-1}R\pi_{*}(\mathcal{C}(k))=0. Since, k≥−1k\geq-1 we have that H1​R​π∗​(𝒪⁡(k))=0H^{1}R\pi_{*}(\mathcal{O}(k))=0 and thus H1​R​π∗​(𝒞⁡(k))=0H^{1}R\pi_{*}(\mathcal{C}(k))=0. Moreover, in Section 3.1, we see that H0​R​π∗​(𝒞⁡(k))H^{0}R\pi_{*}(\mathcal{C}(k)) is locally free. Thus since all Hi​R​π∗​(𝒞⁡(k))H^{i}R\pi_{*}(\mathcal{C}(k)) are flat, by [11, Corollaire 6.9.9], we have that cohomology and base change commute. ∎

In the case that ff is a free form, we could have defined ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} as a free rank nn 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module using the multiplication table given by Equation (2) and ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} for −1≤k≤n−1-1\leq k\leq n-1 as a free rank nn 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module using the action tables for the Equation (3) and (5) bases. (See Section 2.2 for more details.) Both the constructions from hypercohomology described above and from the multiplication and action tables commute with base change. Thus by verification on the universal form (the proof of Theorem 2.7 works over ℤ⁡[f0,…,fn]{\mathbb{Z}}[f_{0},\dots,f_{n}]) we see, as in Theorem 2.10, that for free binary forms and −1≤k≤n−1-1\leq k\leq n-1, these two definitions of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} and ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} agree.

For any ll, we can also formulate this theory for ll-twisted binary forms f∈SymnV⊗(∧2V)⊗lf\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes l}, where

(9) ℛf:=H0Rπ∗(𝒪(−n)⊗(π∗∧2V)⊗−l→f𝒪),{\mathcal{R}_{f}}:=H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n)\otimes(\pi^{*}\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes-l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}\right),

and

(10) ℐfk:=H0Rπ∗(𝒪(−n+k)⊗(π∗∧2V)⊗−l→f𝒪(k)){\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}:=H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\otimes(\pi^{*}\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes-l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(k)\right)\,

or

(11) ℐfk′:=H0Rπ∗(𝒪(−n+k)⊗(π∗∧2V)→f𝒪(k)⊗(π∗∧2V)⊗l+1).{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}^{\prime}:=H^{0}R\pi_{*}\left(\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\otimes(\pi^{*}\wedge^{2}V)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(k)\otimes(\pi^{*}\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes l+1}\right).

By the projection formula, ℐfk′=ℐfk⊗(∧2V)⊗l+1{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}^{\prime}={\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes l+1}. By an argument analogous to that of Theorem 3.2 we find that these constructions also commute with base change for −1≤k≤n−1-1\leq k\leq n-1. Note that since SymnV⊗(∧2V)⊗l≅SymnV∗⊗(∧2V∗)⊗−n−l\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes l}\cong\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}V^{*})^{\otimes-n-l} (see Lemmas B.3 and B.4 in the Appendix), the theory of ll-twisted binary nn-ic forms is equivalent to the theory of (−n−l)(-n-l)-twisted binary nn-ic forms.

3.1 Long exact sequence of cohomology

In this section, we use the long exact sequence of cohomology to find the 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module structures of the rings and modules we have constructed, and important relationships between these 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module structures. From the short exact sequence of complexes in degrees -1 and 0

(12) 𝒪⁡(k)↓𝒪⁡(−n+k)→f𝒪⁡(k)↓𝒪⁡(−n+k)\begin{CD}\mathcal{O}(k)\\ @V{}V{}V\\ \mathcal{O}(-n+k)@>{f}>{}>\mathcal{O}(k)\\ @V{}V{}V\\ \mathcal{O}(-n+k)\end{CD}

(where each complex is on a horizontal line), we have the long exact sequence of cohomology

H0​R​π∗​𝒪​(−n+k)→H0​R​π∗​𝒪​(k)→H0​R​π∗\displaystyle H^{0}R\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\rightarrow H^{0}R\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}(k)\rightarrow H^{0}R\pi_{*} (𝒪⁡(−n+k)→f𝒪⁡(k))\displaystyle\left(\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(k)\right)
→H1​R​π∗​𝒪​(−n+k)→H1​R​π∗​𝒪​(k).\displaystyle\rightarrow H^{1}R\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\rightarrow H^{1}R\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}(k).

For k≤n−1k\leq n-1, we have H0​R​π∗​𝒪​(−n+k)=0H^{0}R\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}(-n+k)=0 and for k≥−1k\geq-1 we have H1​R​π∗​𝒪​(k)=0H^{1}R\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}(k)=0. Also, H0​R​π∗​𝒪​(k)=Symk⁡VH^{0}R\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}(k)=\operatorname{Sym}^{k}V and H1Rπ∗𝒪(−n+k)=(Symn−k−2V)∗⊗(∧2V)∗.H^{1}R\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}(-n+k)=(\operatorname{Sym}^{n-k-2}V)^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{*}. Thus for 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1 and a binary form f∈Symn⁡Vf\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V, we have the exact sequence

(13) 0→SymkV→ℐfk→(Symn−k−2V)∗⊗(∧2V)∗→0.0\rightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^{k}V\rightarrow{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}\rightarrow(\operatorname{Sym}^{n-k-2}V)^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{*}\rightarrow 0.

Thus ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} has a canonical rank k+1k+1 𝒪S\mathcal{O}_{S}-module inside of it (coming from the global sections xk,xk−1​y,…,ykx^{k},x^{k-1}y,\dots,y^{k} of 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k)), and a canonical rank n−k−1n-k-1 𝒪S\mathcal{O}_{S}-module quotient.

So we see, for example, that as an 𝒪S\mathcal{O}_{S}-module

ℛf/𝒪S≅(Symn−2V)∗⊗(∧2V)∗.{\mathcal{R}_{f}}/\mathcal{O}_{S}\cong(\operatorname{Sym}^{n-2}V)^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{*}.

Note that if we make the corresponding exact sequence for an ll-twisted binary form f∈SymnV⊗(∧2V)⊗lf\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes l} we have

(14) 0→SymkV→ℐfk→(Symn−k−2V)∗⊗(∧2V)⊗−l−1→00\rightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^{k}V\rightarrow{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}\rightarrow(\operatorname{Sym}^{n-k-2}V)^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes-l-1}\rightarrow 0

or

(15) 0→SymkV⊗(∧2V)⊗l+1→ℐfk′→(Symn−k−2V)∗→0.0\rightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^{k}V\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes l+1}\rightarrow{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}^{\prime}\rightarrow(\operatorname{Sym}^{n-k-2}V)^{*}\rightarrow 0.

In Section 2.1 we have given a multiplication table for an explicit basis of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} and an (implicit) action table for an explicit basis of ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}. One naturally wonders how those bases relate to the exact sequences that we have just found. Consider the universal form ff over the base ring B=ℤ⁡[f0,…,fn]B={\mathbb{Z}}[f_{0},\dots,f_{n}]. We can use the concrete construction of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} and ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} in Section 2.1. If KK is the fraction field of BB, then the concrete constructions of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} and ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} lie in Qf:=K⁡(θ)/(f0​θn+f1​θn−1+⋯+fn)Q_{f}:=K(\theta)/(f_{0}\theta^{n}+f_{1}\theta^{n-1}+\dots+f_{n}) and are given by Equations (1) and (3).

Proposition 3.3.

For the universal form ff, where VV is a free module on xx and yy, in the exact sequence of Equation (14) or Equation (15) (with ∧2V\wedge^{2}V trivialized by the basis element x∧yx\wedge y) we have that

xi​yk−i∈Symk⁡V​ is identified with ​θi∈ℐfk​ for ​0≤i≤kx^{i}y^{k-i}\in\operatorname{Sym}^{k}V\text{ is identified with }\theta^{i}\in{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}\text{ for }0\leq i\leq k

and

the dual basis to ​xn−k−i−1​yi−1∈Symn−k−2⁡V​ is identified with \text{the dual basis to }x^{n-k-i-1}y^{i-1}\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n-k-2}V\text{ is identified with }
ζk+i∈ℐfk​ for ​1≤i≤n−k−1.\zeta_{k+i}\in{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}\text{ for }1\leq i\leq n-k-1.
Proof.

For the universal form, the cohomological construction simplifies. We can replace the complex 𝒪⁡(−n+k)→𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\rightarrow\mathcal{O}(k) on ℙB1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{B} with the single sheaf 𝒪⁡(k)/f⁡(𝒪⁡(−n+k))\mathcal{O}(k)/f(\mathcal{O}(-n+k)). We can then replace Hi​R​π∗H^{i}R\pi_{*} with HiH^{i} since the base is affine. The short exact sequence of complexes in Equation (12) then simplifies to the short exact sequence of sheaves

0→𝒪⁡(−n+k)→f𝒪⁡(k)→𝒪⁡(k)/f⁡(𝒪⁡(−n+k))→0,0\rightarrow\mathcal{O}(-n+k)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}(k)\rightarrow\mathcal{O}(k)/f(\mathcal{O}(-n+k))\rightarrow 0,

which gives the same long exact sequence leading to Equation (13). The identification of ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} with global sections is at the end of proof of Theorem 2.7, and from that it is easy to see that the map H0​(ℙB1,𝒪⁡(k))→H0​(ℙB1,𝒪⁡(k)/f⁡(𝒪⁡(−n+k)))=ℐfkH^{0}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{B},\mathcal{O}(k))\rightarrow H^{0}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{B},\mathcal{O}(k)/f(\mathcal{O}(-n+k)))={\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} sends xi​yk−i↦θix^{i}y^{k-i}\mapsto\theta^{i}. To compute the δ\delta map ℐfk→H1​(ℙB1,𝒪⁡(−n+k)){\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}\rightarrow H^{1}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{B},\mathcal{O}(-n+k)), we will next use Cech cohomology for the usual affine cover of ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} and the δ\delta map is the snake lemma map between rows of the Cech complexes.

In the notation of Theorem 2.7, the element ζk+i\zeta_{k+i} is identified with the global section ziz_{i}. The global function ziz_{i} pulls back to zi∈Γ⁡(Ux,𝒪⁡(k))×Γ⁡(Uy,𝒪⁡(k))z_{i}\in\Gamma(U_{x},\mathcal{O}(k))\times\Gamma(U_{y},\mathcal{O}(k)) which maps to f/(xn−k−i​yi)∈Γ⁡(Ux∩Uy,𝒪⁡(k))f/(x^{n-k-i}y^{i})\in\Gamma(U_{x}\cap U_{y},\mathcal{O}(k)). This pulls back to 1/(xn−k−i​yi)∈Γ⁡(Ux∩Uy,𝒪⁡(−n+k))1/(x^{n-k-i}y^{i})\in\Gamma(U_{x}\cap U_{y},\mathcal{O}(-n+k)), which in the standard pairing of the cohomology of projective space (e.g. in [12, III, Theorem 5.1]) pairs with xn−k−i−1​yi−1∈H0​(ℙB1,𝒪⁡(n−k−2))≅Symn−k−2⁡Vx^{n-k-i-1}y^{i-1}\in H^{0}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{B},\mathcal{O}(n-k-2))\cong\operatorname{Sym}_{n-k-2}V. ∎

Since the ring ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} acts on ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}, it is natural to want to understand this action in terms of the exact sequences of Equation  (14). We have the following description, which can be proved purely formally by the cohomological constructions of everything involved. Alternatively, with the concrete description of the basis elements in Proposition 3.3, one could prove the following by computation.

Proposition 3.4.

The map ℛf/𝒪S⊗SymkV→Symn−k−2V∗⊗(∧2V)⊗−l−1{\mathcal{R}_{f}}/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{k}V\rightarrow\operatorname{Sym}_{n-k-2}V^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes-l-1} given by the action of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} on ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k} and the exact sequence of Equation  (14) is identified with the natural map (see Lemma B.2 in the Appendix)

under the identification R/𝒪S≅Symn−2V∗⊗(∧2V)⊗−l−1R/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\cong\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}V^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes-l-1} of Equation (14). The map ℛf/𝒪S⊗SymkV⊗(∧2V)⊗l+1→Symn−k−2V∗{\mathcal{R}_{f}}/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{k}V\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes l+1}\rightarrow\operatorname{Sym}_{n-k-2}V^{*} given by the action of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} on ℐfk′{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}^{\prime} and the exact sequence of Equation  (15) is identified with the natural map (see Lemma B.2 in the Appendix)

Symn−2V∗⊗(∧2V)⊗−l−1⊗SymkV⊗(∧2V)⊗l+1→Symn−k−2V∗\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}V^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes-l-1}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{k}V\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes l+1}\rightarrow\operatorname{Sym}_{n-k-2}V^{*}

under the identification R/𝒪S≅Symn−2V∗⊗(∧2V)⊗−l−1R/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\cong\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}V^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}V)^{\otimes-l-1} of Equation (14).

3.2 Dual modules

For −1≤k≤n−1-1\leq k\leq n-1 we have a map

(16) ℐfk′⊗ℐfn−2−k→ℐfn−2′→𝒪S.{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\prime}_{k}\otimes{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-2-k}\rightarrow{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\prime}_{n-2}\rightarrow{\mathcal{O}_{S}}.

The first map is induced from the map from the product of the complexes used to define ℐfk′{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\prime}_{k} and ℐfn−2−k{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-2-k} to the complex used to define ℐfn−2′{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\prime}_{n-2}. The second map comes from Equation (15).

Theorem 3.5.

The pairing in Equation (16) gives an 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module map

ℐfk′→ℐfn−2−k∗,{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}^{\prime}\rightarrow{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{*}_{n-2-k},

and this map is an ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-module isomorphism.

Proof.

We will show that this map is an ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-module isomorphism by checking on the universal form. Since all forms are locally a pull-back from the universal form and these constructions commute with base change, the theorem will follow for all forms.

We use the construction of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} and ℐfk′{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\prime}_{k} and ℐfn−2−k{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-2-k} in Section 2.1. (Note that for the universal form, we trivialize all ∧2V\wedge^{2}V with the basis x∧yx\wedge y and so ℐfk′=ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\prime}_{k}={\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}.) Since the complex used to define ℐfi{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{i} is chain homotopy equivalent to the sheaf 𝒪⁡(i)/f⁡(𝒪⁡(i−n))\mathcal{O}(i)/f(\mathcal{O}(i-n)), we see that the map ℐfk′⊗ℐfn−2−k→ℐfn−2′{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\prime}_{k}\otimes{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-2-k}\rightarrow{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\prime}_{n-2} is just the multiplication of global sections of 𝒪​(k)Sf\mathcal{O}(k)_{S_{f}} and 𝒪​(n−2−k)Sf\mathcal{O}(n-2-k)_{S_{f}} to obtain a global section of 𝒪​(n−2)Sf\mathcal{O}(n-2)_{S_{f}}. This can be realized by multiplication of elements of the fractional ideals ℐfk{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}, ℐfn−2−k{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-2-k}, and ℐfn−2{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-2} in Section 2.1.

Lemma 3.6.

Consider the 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module basis

1,θ,…,θk,ζk+1+fk+1,…,ζn−1+fn−11,\theta,\dots,\theta^{k},\zeta_{k+1}+f_{k+1},\dots,\zeta_{n-1}+f_{n-1}

for ℐfk′{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}^{\prime}. For ℐfn−2−k{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-2-k}, consider the 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module basis of Equation (4), but reverse the order to obtain

f0​θn−1+f1​θn−2+⋯+fk​θn−k−1,…,f0​θn−k+f1​θn−k−1,f0​θn−k−1,θn−2−k,…,θ,1.f_{0}\theta^{n-1}+f_{1}\theta^{n-2}+\dots+f_{k}\theta^{n-k-1},\dots,f_{0}\theta^{n-k}+f_{1}\theta^{n-k-1},f_{0}\theta^{n-k-1},\theta^{n-2-k},\dots,\theta,1.

These are dual basis with respect to the pairing from Equation (16).

Proof.

From Proposition 3.3, we know that the map ϕ:ℐfn−2′→𝒪S\phi:{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{\prime}_{n-2}\rightarrow{\mathcal{O}_{S}} in Equation (15) sends ζn−1↦1\zeta_{n-1}\mapsto 1 and θi↦0\theta^{i}\mapsto 0 for 0≤i≤n−20\leq i\leq n-2. The proof of this lemma then has four cases.

Case 1: We see that θi​θj↦ϕ0\theta^{i}\theta^{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\phi}}{{\mapsto}}0 if 0≤i≤k0\leq i\leq k and 0≤j≤n−2−k0\leq j\leq n-2-k.

(ζi+fi)​(f0​θj+⋯+fj+k+1−n​θn−k−1)=(ζi​θn−i+fi​θn−i)​(f0​θj+i−n+⋯+fj+k+1−n​θi−k−1)\displaystyle(\zeta_{i}+f_{i})(f_{0}\theta^{j}+\dots+f_{j+k+1-n}\theta^{n-k-1})=(\zeta_{i}\theta^{n-i}+f_{i}\theta^{n-i})(f_{0}\theta^{j+i-n}+\dots+f_{j+k+1-n}\theta^{i-k-1})
=(−fi+1​θn−i−1−⋯−fn)​(f0​θj+i−n+⋯+fj+k+1−n​θi−k−1).\displaystyle=(-f_{i+1}\theta^{n-i-1}-\dots-f_{n})(f_{0}\theta^{j+i-n}+\dots+f_{j+k+1-n}\theta^{i-k-1}).

Since n−i−1+j+i−n=j−1≤n−2n-i-1+j+i-n=j-1\leq n-2, we see that

(ζi+fi)​(f0​θj+⋯+fj+k+1−n​θn−k−1)↦ϕ0.(\zeta_{i}+f_{i})(f_{0}\theta^{j}+\dots+f_{j+k+1-n}\theta^{n-k-1})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\phi}}{{\mapsto}}0.

Case 3: We compute the image of θi​(f0​θj+⋯+fj+k+1−n​θn−k−1)\theta^{i}(f_{0}\theta^{j}+\dots+f_{j+k+1-n}\theta^{n-k-1}) under ϕ\phi for 0≤i≤k0\leq i\leq k and n−k−1≤j≤n−1n-k-1\leq j\leq n-1.

  • •

    If i+j≤n−2i+j\leq n-2, this maps to 0.

  • •

    If i+j=n−1i+j=n-1, this maps to 1.

  • •

    If i+j≥ni+j\geq n, the product is

    f0​θj+i+⋯+fj+k+1−n​θn−k−1+i=−fj+k+2−n​θn−k−2+i−⋯−fn​θi+j−n,f_{0}\theta^{j+i}+\dots+f_{j+k+1-n}\theta^{n-k-1+i}=-f_{j+k+2-n}\theta^{n-k-2+i}-\dots-f_{n}\theta^{i+j-n},

    and since n−k−2+i≤n−2n-k-2+i\leq n-2 it maps to 0.

Case 4: We compute the image of (ζi+fi)​θj(\zeta_{i}+f_{i})\theta^{j} under ϕ\phi for k+1≤i≤n−1k+1\leq i\leq n-1 and 0≤j≤n−2−k0\leq j\leq n-2-k.

    If i+j≤n−2i+j\leq n-2, this maps to 0.

Finally, it is easy to see in the universal case that the pairing gives an ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-module homomorphism ℐfk′→ℐfn−2−k∗,{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{k}^{\prime}\rightarrow{\mathcal{I}_{f}}^{*}_{n-2-k}, since the pairing factors through multiplication of the fractional ideal elements.

∎

Let ff be an ll-twisted binary nn-ic form over a base scheme SS. Then we have an isomorphism of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}-modules

ℐfn−2′≅ℋ​o​m𝒪S​(ℛf,𝒪S){\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-2}^{\prime}\cong\mathcal{H}om_{\mathcal{O}_{S}}({\mathcal{R}_{f}},{\mathcal{O}_{S}})

given by j↦(r↦ϕ⁡(r​j))j\mapsto(r\mapsto\phi(rj)) where ϕ:ℐfn−2′→𝒪S\phi:{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-2}^{\prime}\rightarrow{\mathcal{O}_{S}} is the map from Equation (15).

4 Main Theorem for (−1)(-1)-twisted binary forms

In this section, we will see how a binary form is actually equivalent to a certain combination of the data we have constructed from it. Let ff be a (−1)(-1)-twisted binary form over a base scheme SS. Let R=ℛfR={\mathcal{R}_{f}}, let I=ℐfn−3I={\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-3}, and let I→QI\rightarrow Q be the canonical quotient of ℐfn−3{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-3} from Equation (14). So, Q≅V∗Q\cong V^{*}. From Proposition 3.4, we know that the map R/𝒪S⊗Symn−3⁡Q∗→QR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\rightarrow Q given by the action of RR on II and the exact sequence of Equation (14) is identified with the natural map Symn−2⁡Q⊗Symn−3⁡Q∗→Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\rightarrow Q under the identification R/𝒪S≅Symn−2⁡QR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\cong\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q of Equation (14).

Definition. A binary nn-pair is an 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-algebra RR, an RR-module II, an exact sequence 0→Symn−3⁡Q∗→I→Q→00\rightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\rightarrow I\rightarrow Q\rightarrow 0 such that QQ is a locally free rank 22 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module, and an isomorphism R/𝒪S≅Symn−2⁡QR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\cong\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q that identifies the map R/𝒪S⊗Symn−3⁡Q∗→QR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\rightarrow Q induced from the action of RR on II with the natural map Symn−2⁡Q⊗Symn−3⁡Q∗→Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\rightarrow Q.

Remark 4.1.

When n=3n=3, we have that ker⁡(I→Q)≅𝒪S\ker(I\rightarrow Q)\cong{\mathcal{O}_{S}} and the map Q⊗𝒪S→QQ\otimes{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\rightarrow Q given by the ring action R/𝒪S⊗ker⁡(I→Q)→QR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\otimes\ker(I\rightarrow Q)\rightarrow Q is just the natural one. We can tensor the exact sequence 0→𝒪S→R→R/𝒪S→00\rightarrow{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\rightarrow R\rightarrow R/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\rightarrow 0 with ker⁡(I→Q)\ker(I\rightarrow Q) to show that R≅IR\cong I as RR-modules. We can conclude that a binary 3-pair is just equivalent to a cubic ring, i.e. an 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-algebra RR that is a locally free rank 3 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module.

There are two equivalent formulations of the definition of a binary pair that can be useful.

Proposition 4.2.

An 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-algebra RR and and RR-module II are in a a binary pair with QQ a free 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module if and only if RR has a 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module basis ζ0=1,ζ1,…,ζn−1\zeta_{0}=1,\zeta_{1},\dots,\zeta_{n-1} and and II has a 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module basis α1,α2,β1,…,βn−2\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{n-2} such that

the αi coefficient of ζj​βk is ​{1if i+j+k=n+1 0otherwise.\text{the $\alpha_{i}$ coefficient of $\zeta_{j}\beta_{k}$ is }\begin{cases}1&\text{if $i+j+k=n+1$ }\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
Proof.

If QQ is free with basis x,yx,y and dual basis x˙\dot{x} and y˙\dot{y} , we can explicitly calculate the natural map Symn−2⁡Q⊗Symn−3⁡Q∗→Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\rightarrow Q. Let sym⁡(w)\operatorname{sym}(w) of a word ww be the sum of all distinct permutations of ww. We have that

sym⁡(xi​yn−2−i)⊗x˙j​y˙n−3−j↦{xif i=j+1 yif i=j 0otherwise.\operatorname{sym}(x^{i}y^{n-2-i})\otimes\dot{x}^{j}\dot{y}^{n-3-j}\mapsto\begin{cases}x&\text{if $i=j+1$ }\\ y&\text{if $i=j$ }\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

We have ζj∈Symn−2⁡Q\zeta_{j}\in\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q corresponding to sym⁡(xn−j−1​yj−1)\operatorname{sym}(x^{n-j-1}y^{j-1}), and α1\alpha_{1} corresponding to yy and α2\alpha_{2} corresponding to xx, and βk\beta_{k} corresponding to x˙k−1​y˙n−2−k\dot{x}^{k-1}\dot{y}^{n-2-k}, and we obtain the proposition. ∎

Proposition 4.3.

An 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-algebra RR, an RR-module II, a locally free rank 2 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module QQ that is a quotient of II, and an isomorphism of 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-modules ϕ:Symn−2⁡Q≅R/𝒪S\phi:\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\cong R/{\mathcal{O}_{S}} are in binary pair if and only if

0⟶Symn−1⁡Q⟶Q⊗Symn−2⁡Q⟶(ker(I→Q))∗⊗∧2Q⟶0q1q2⋯qn−1↦q1⊗q2⋯qn−1↦q⊗q1⋯qn−2↦(k↦q∧ϕ(q1⋯qn−2)∘k)\begin{array}[]{ccccccccc}0&\longrightarrow&\operatorname{Sym}_{n-1}Q&\longrightarrow&Q\otimes\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q&\longrightarrow&\left(\ker(I\rightarrow Q)\right)^{*}\otimes\wedge^{2}Q&\longrightarrow&0\\ &&q_{1}q_{2}\cdots q_{n-1}&\mapsto&q_{1}\otimes q_{2}\cdots q_{n-1}&\mapsto&&&\\ &&&&q\otimes q_{1}\cdots q_{n-2}&\mapsto&\left(k\mapsto q\wedge\phi(q_{1}\cdots q_{n-2})\circ k\right)&&\end{array}

is an exact sequence, where ∘\circ denotes the action of RR on II followed by the quotient to QQ..

Proposition 4.3 follows from the following Lemma, proven in Lemma B.5 of the Appendix (Section B).

Lemma 4.4.

If QQ is any locally free rank 2 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module, we have the exact sequence

0⟶Symn−1⁡Q⟶Q⊗Symn−2⁡Q⟶Symn−3Q⊗∧2Q⟶0.q1q2⋯qn−1↦q1⊗q2⋯qn−1↦q2⋯qn−2⊗(qn−1∧q1)\begin{array}[]{ccccccccc}0&\longrightarrow&\operatorname{Sym}_{n-1}Q&\longrightarrow&Q\otimes\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q&\longrightarrow&\operatorname{Sym}_{n-3}Q\otimes\wedge^{2}Q&\longrightarrow&0.\\ &&q_{1}q_{2}\cdots q_{n-1}&\mapsto&q_{1}\otimes q_{2}\cdots q_{n-1}&\mapsto&q_{2}\cdots q_{n-2}\otimes(q_{n-1}\wedge q_{1})&&\end{array}

The following lemma is used to construct a (−1)(-1)-twisted binary form from a binary pair, and is proven in Lemma B.6 of the Appendix (Section B).

Lemma 4.5.

Let RR be an 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-algebra, II be an RR-module, QQ be a locally free rank 2 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module quotient of II, and ϕ\phi be an isomorphism of 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-modules ϕ:Symn−2⁡Q≅R/𝒪S\phi:\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\cong R/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}. If

Symn−1⁡Q⊗ker⁡(I→Q)⟶∧2Qq1⋯qn−1⊗k↦q1∧ϕ(q2⋯qn−1)∘k\begin{array}[]{ccc}\operatorname{Sym}_{n-1}Q\otimes\ker(I\rightarrow Q)&\longrightarrow&\wedge^{2}Q\\ q_{1}\cdots q_{n-1}\otimes k&\mapsto&q_{1}\wedge\phi(q_{2}\cdots q_{n-1})\circ k\end{array}

is the zero map, then

Symn⁡Q⟶∧2Qq1⋯qn↦q1∧ϕ(q2⋯qn−1)∘qn~\begin{array}[]{ccc}\operatorname{Sym}_{n}Q&\longrightarrow&\wedge^{2}Q\\ q_{1}\cdots q_{n}&\mapsto&q_{1}\wedge\phi(q_{2}\cdots q_{n-1})\circ\tilde{q_{n}}\end{array}

is well-defined. Here the ∘\circ denotes the action of RR on II followed by the quotient to QQ and q~\tilde{q} denotes a fixed splitting Q→IQ\rightarrow I. In particular the map SymnQ→∧2Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n}Q\rightarrow\wedge^{2}Q does not depend on the choice of this splitting.

By Proposition 4.3, we see that Symn−1Q⊗ker(I→Q)→∧2Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n-1}Q\otimes\ker(I\rightarrow Q)\rightarrow\wedge^{2}Q is always the zero map for a binary pair, and thus we can use Lemma 4.5 to construct a (−1)(-1)-twisted binary form in SymnQ∗⊗∧2Q\operatorname{Sym}^{n}Q^{*}\otimes\wedge^{2}Q from a binary pair. We can write the map of Lemma 4.5 as the evaluation

x↦x∧ϕ⁡(xn−2)​xx\mapsto x\wedge\phi(x^{n-2})x

of a degree nn map Q→∧2QQ\rightarrow\wedge^{2}Q. Note this coincides with the map x∧x2x\wedge x^{2} as described in the case of binary cubic forms in [1, Footnote 3].

Theorem 4.6.

Let (V,f)(V,f) be a (−1)(-1)-twisted binary form and (R,I)(R,I) be its associated binary pair. The (−1)(-1)-twisted binary form constructed from (R,I)(R,I) is f∈SymnV⊗∧2Vf\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V\otimes\wedge^{2}V.

Proof.

First we note that the (−1)(-1)-twisted binary form constructed from (R,I)(R,I) is a global section of SymnV⊗∧2V\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V\otimes\wedge^{2}V. Then, we can check the theorem locally on SS, so we can assume that ff is a free form. Since ff then is a pull-back from the universal form, we can just check the theorem on the universal form ff over B=ℤ⁡[f0,…,fn]B={\mathbb{Z}}[f_{0},\dots,f_{n}]. Let x,yx,y be the basis of Q≅V∗Q\cong V^{*} and x˙,y˙\dot{x},\dot{y} be a corresponding dual basis.

The (−1)(-1)-twisted binary nn-ic form associated to our binary nn-pair is given by

Symn⁡Q⟶∧2Qq1⋯qn↦q1∧ϕ(q2⋯qn−1)∘qn~.\begin{array}[]{ccc}\operatorname{Sym}_{n}Q&\longrightarrow&\wedge^{2}Q\\ q_{1}\cdots q_{n}&\mapsto&q_{1}\wedge\phi(q_{2}\cdots q_{n-1})\circ\tilde{q_{n}}\end{array}.

Thus for 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n we have

sym⁡(xk​yn−k)\displaystyle\operatorname{sym}(x^{k}y^{n-k}) ↦x∧ϕ⁡(sym⁡(xk−2​yn−k))​x+x∧ϕ⁡(sym⁡(xk−1​yn−k−1))​y\displaystyle\mapsto x\wedge\phi(\operatorname{sym}(x^{k-2}y^{n-k}))x+x\wedge\phi(\operatorname{sym}(x^{k-1}y^{n-k-1}))y
+y∧ϕ⁡(sym⁡(xk−1​yn−k−1))​x+y∧ϕ⁡(sym⁡(xk​yn−k−2))​y\displaystyle+y\wedge\phi(\operatorname{sym}(x^{k-1}y^{n-k-1}))x+y\wedge\phi(\operatorname{sym}(x^{k}y^{n-k-2}))y
(17) =\displaystyle= (y˙​(ζn−k+1​x)+y˙​(ζn−k​y)−x˙​(ζn−k​x)−x˙​(ζn−k−1​y))⊗(x∧y)\displaystyle(\dot{y}(\zeta_{n-k+1}x)+\dot{y}(\zeta_{n-k}y)-\dot{x}(\zeta_{n-k}x)-\dot{x}(\zeta_{n-k-1}y))\otimes(x\wedge y)

where by convention sym⁡(xa​yb)\operatorname{sym}(x^{a}y^{b}) is zero if either aa or bb is negative and ζi=0\zeta_{i}=0 if i<1i<1 or i>n−1i>n-1. If KK is the fraction field of BB, then the concrete constructions of ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}} and ℐfn−3{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-3} from Section 2.1 lie in Qf:=K⁡(θ)/(f0​θn+f1​θn−1+⋯+fn)Q_{f}:=K(\theta)/(f_{0}\theta^{n}+f_{1}\theta^{n-1}+\dots+f_{n}) and are given by Equations (1) and (3).
