In fact, we have the following theorem, which shows that (−1)(-1)-twisted binary forms exactly parametrize binary pairs.

Theorem 4.7.

For n≥3,n\geq 3, we have a bijection between (−1)(-1)-twisted binary nn-ic forms over SS and binary nn-pairs over SS, and the bijection commutes with base change in SS. In other words, we have a isomorphism of the moduli stack of (−1)(-1)-twisted binary nn-ic forms and the moduli stack of binary nn-pairs.

An isomorphism of two (−1)(-1)-twisted binary nn-ic forms f∈SymnV⊗∧2V∗f\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V\otimes\wedge^{2}V^{*} and f′∈SymnV′⊗∧2(V′)∗f^{\prime}\in\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V^{\prime}\otimes\wedge^{2}(V^{\prime})^{*} is an isomorphism V≅V′V\cong V^{\prime} that preserves ff. An isomorphism of two binary nn-pairs RR, II, QQ and R′,R^{\prime}, I′I^{\prime}, Q′Q^{\prime} is given by isomorphisms R≅R′R\cong R^{\prime}, and I≅I′I\cong I^{\prime}, and Q≅Q′Q\cong Q^{\prime} that respect the exact sequence for II (and I′I^{\prime}) and the maps R/𝒪S≅Symn−2⁡QR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\cong\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q and R′/𝒪S≅Symn−2⁡Q′R^{\prime}/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\cong\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q^{\prime}.

See [22] for the full story for binary quadratic forms. In the n=3n=3 case, from Remark 4.1 we know that a binary 3-pair is equivalent to a cubic ring, an 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-algebra RR such that RR is a locally free rank 3 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module. Thus we obtain the following corollary, given in [7] (see also [24] for a detailed exposition of this case).

Corollary 4.8.

We have a bijection between (−1)(-1)-twisted binary cubic forms over SS and cubic rings over SS, and the bijection commutes with base change in SS. In other words, we have a isomorphism of the moduli stack of (−1)(-1)-twisted binary nn-ic forms and the moduli stack of cubic rings.

To prove Theorem 4.7 we will rigidify the moduli stacks, and thus we will need to define based binary pairs.

4.1 Based binary pairs

A based binary pair is binary pair R,I,QR,I,Q and a choice of basis x,yx,y of QQ such that QQ is the free 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module on xx and yy. This gives a natural basis of R/𝒪SR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}} as a free rank (n−1)(n-1) 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module, and thus RR is a free rank nn 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module. Let K=(Symn−3⁡Q)∗=ker⁡(I→Q)K=(\operatorname{Sym}_{n-3}Q)^{*}=\ker(I\rightarrow Q), and so we have a natural basis for KK as a free rank n−2n-2 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module. Thus II is a free rank nn 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module. However, we do not yet have canonical bases for RR and II as 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-modules. We will pick these using certain normalizations.

Let ζi=sym⁡(xn−1−i​yi−1)\zeta_{i}=\operatorname{sym}(x^{n-1-i}y^{i-1}) for 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\ \leq n-1 be the given basis of R/𝒪SR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}} and let kjk_{j} for 1≤j≤n−21\leq j\ \leq n-2 be the given basis of KK dual to the basis sym⁡xj−1​yn−2−j\operatorname{sym}{x^{j-1}y^{n-2-j}} of Symn−3⁡Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n-3}Q. Let x˙,y˙∈Q∗\dot{x},\dot{y}\in Q^{*} be a dual basis of x,yx,y. (Recall that sym⁡(w)\operatorname{sym}(w) for a word ww is the sum of all distinct permutations of ww.) Thus from Proposition 4.2,

(18) the image of ​ζi​kj​ in Q is ​{xif i+j=n−1 yif i+j=n0otherwise.\text{the image of }\zeta_{i}k_{j}\textrm{ in $Q$ is }\begin{cases}x&\text{if $i+j=n-1$ }\\ y&\text{if $i+j=n$}\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Equation (18) allows us to choose normalized lifts of xx and yy to elements of II that forms a basis along with the given basis of KK, and normalized lifts of the ζi\zeta_{i} to RR to form a basis along with 11. We choose these lifts so that

(19) y˙​(ζi​x)=0​ for ​2≤i≤n−1\dot{y}(\zeta_{i}x)=0\text{ for }2\leq i\leq n-1

by changing the lift xx by an appropriate multiple of kn−ik_{n-i}. We then specify that

(20) x˙​(ζi​x)=0​ for ​1≤i≤n−1\dot{x}(\zeta_{i}x)=0\text{ for }1\leq i\leq n-1

by changing the lift of ζi\zeta_{i} by an appropriate multiple of 11. Finally, we specify that

(21) y˙​(ζi​y)=0​ for ​2≤i≤n−1\dot{y}(\zeta_{i}y)=0\text{ for }2\leq i\leq n-1

by changing the lift of yy by an appropriate multiple of kn−ik_{n-i}. These specifications determine a unique lift of xx and yy to II, and unique lifts of the ζi\zeta_{i} to RR, which we will refer to now as simply xx, yy, and ζi\zeta_{i}. We will now see that with these choices of normalized bases for RR and II, we can determine the action of RR and II in terms of a small number of variables, and these variables will in fact be the coefficients of the binary form associated to this binary pair.

There are only n+1n+1 coordinates we have not determined in the maps ζi:I→Q\zeta_{i}:I\rightarrow Q. Equation (18) gives ζi:K→Q\zeta_{i}:K\rightarrow Q. Our choice of normalization gives all but the following. Let −ai+1=x˙​(ζi​y)-a_{i+1}=\dot{x}(\zeta_{i}y) for 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1. Let a0=y˙​(ζ1​x)a_{0}=\dot{y}(\zeta_{1}x) and a1=y˙​(ζ1​y)a_{1}=\dot{y}(\zeta_{1}y). These aia_{i} specify the map ζi:I→Q\zeta_{i}:I\rightarrow Q. We have carefully indexed and signed the aia_{i} so that we have the following.

Proposition 4.9.

The (−1)(-1)-twisted binary form associated to the above based binary pair is

Symn⁡Q⟶∧2Qsym⁡(xk​yn−k)↦an−k​x∧y.\begin{array}[]{ccc}\operatorname{Sym}_{n}Q&\longrightarrow&\wedge^{2}Q\\ \operatorname{sym}(x^{k}y^{n-k})&\mapsto&a_{n-k}x\wedge y\end{array}.
Proof.

We use the formula from Equation (17). ∎

Moreover, we find that the coefficients of the associated (−1)(-1)-twisted binary form determine the based binary pair.

Proposition 4.10.

The maps ζi:R→I\zeta_{i}:R\rightarrow I and ζi:R→R\zeta_{i}:R\rightarrow R are determined by the maps ζi:I→Q\zeta_{i}:I\rightarrow Q and the commutativity relations on the ζi\zeta_{i}. Each coordinate of the action and multiplication maps is as a polynomial in the aia_{i} with integral coefficients.

Proof.

We view each map ζi:R→I\zeta_{i}:R\rightarrow I as an nn by nn matrix ZiZ_{i}. We write Zi​(a,b)Z_{i}(a,b) for the a,ba,b entry of ZiZ_{i}, which is the kak_{a} coordinate of ζi​kb\zeta_{i}k_{b}, where by convention kn−1=xk_{n-1}=x and kn=yk_{n}=y. We let 𝒦\mathcal{K} be the set of all of entries of these matrices that are determined by the entries in the last two rows of the matrices as polynomials in the aia_{i} (i.e. the maps ζi:I→Q\zeta_{i}:I\rightarrow Q), as well as as all polynomial combinations of the matrix entries which are so determined. We will show that the systems of equations given by commutativity of the ζi\zeta_{i} determine all the matrix entries from the last two rows. So, by definition we have Zi​(n−1,k),Zi​(n,k)∈𝒦Z_{i}(n-1,k),Z_{i}(n,k)\in\mathcal{K} for 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1 and 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n.

We have two tools that we use to solve for more and more matrix entries.

Lemma 4.11.

We have

Zi​(n−1−ℓ,k)−Zℓ​(n−1−i,k)∈𝒦, for 1≤i≤n−1 and 1≤ℓ≤n−1Z_{i}(n-1-\ell,k)-Z_{\ell}(n-1-i,k)\in\mathcal{K},\quad\text{ for $1\leq i\leq n-1$ and $1\leq\ell\leq n-1$}
Proof.

Consider the n−1n-1st rows (xx coordinates) of Zi​ZℓZ_{i}Z_{\ell} and Zℓ​ZiZ_{\ell}Z_{i}. Equating the jjth entries in both these rows gives the lemma, where by convention Zi​(0,k)=0Z_{i}(0,k)=0. ∎

Lemma 4.12.

We have

Zi(n−ℓ,k)−Zℓ(n−i,k)∈𝒦, for 1≤ℓ≤n−1 and 1≤i≤n−1.Z_{i}(n-\ell,k)-Z_{\ell}(n-i,k)\in\mathcal{K,}\quad\text{ for $1\leq\ell\leq n-1$ and $1\leq i\leq n-1$.}
Proof.

Consider the nnth rows (yy coordinates) of Zi​ZℓZ_{i}Z_{\ell} and Zℓ​ZiZ_{\ell}Z_{i}. Equating the jjth entries in both these rows gives the lemma. ∎

We prove, by induction, that all the entries of ZiZ_{i} are in 𝒦\mathcal{K} for 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1. We can use i=0i=0 as the (trivial) base case. Assuming that all the entries of ZiZ_{i} are in 𝒦\mathcal{K}, we will now show that the entries of Zi+1Z_{i+1} are in 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Using Lemma 4.11, we see that that all matrix entries in the n−1−in-1-ith row are in 𝒦\mathcal{K}. (If i=0i=0 this is by from the definition of 𝒦\mathcal{K}.) Using Lemma 4.12, we conclude all the entries of Zi+1Z_{i+1} are in 𝒦\mathcal{K}, which completes the induction.

This shows the proposition for the maps ζi:R→I\zeta_{i}:R\rightarrow I. From Equation (18), we see that since n≥3n\geq 3, each ZiZ_{i} has a 1 in a matrix entry for which all zjz_{j} for j≠ij\neq i have entry 0. Thus, the action of RR on II gives an injection of RR into the space on nn by nn matrices. To find the ζk\zeta_{k} coordinate of ζi​ζj\zeta_{i}\zeta_{j}, we just have to look at the matrix entry of Zi​ZjZ_{i}Z_{j} where ZkZ_{k} has a 1 and all ZℓZ_{\ell} for ℓ≠k\ell\neq k have a zero. This shows the proposition for the maps ζi:R→I\zeta_{i}:R\rightarrow I. ∎

Now we prove Theorem 4.7.

Proof.

The stack of binary nn-pairs is the quotient of the stack of based binary nn-pairs by the GL2\operatorname{GL}_{2} action given by change of the basis for QQ. Since a based binary nn-pair is given by a0,…,an∈𝒪Sa_{0},\dots,a_{n}\in{\mathcal{O}_{S}}, and we have one such binary pair for every choice of aia_{i}’s (given by the corresponding binary form), the moduli space of based binary nn-pairs is ℤ⁡[a0,…,an]{\mathbb{Z}}[a_{0},\dots,a_{n}], and there is a universal based binary nn-pair.

We have maps between the stack of (−1)(-1)-twisted binary nn-ic forms and binary nn-pairs in both directions, which lift to the rigidified versions of these stacks, the stacks of corresponding based objects. Theorem 4.6 shows that the map from forms to pairs back to forms is the identity. We will show that the other composition of these constructions is the identity by verifying it on the rigidified stacks. If we start with the universal based binary nn-pair, Proposition 4.9 shows that the associated form is the universal binary nn-ic form. From the universal binary nn-ic form we construct some based binary nn-pair (R,I)(R,I), and Proposition 4.10 shows that (R,I)(R,I) is determined from the binary form constructed from it–which is just the universal binary form (since we know going from forms to pairs to forms is the identity). Since the universal based binary nn-pair and (R,I)(R,I) both give the same form, by Proposition 4.10 they are the same. Thus, we have prove there is an isomorphism of the moduli stack of (−1)(-1)-twisted binary nn-ic forms and the moduli stack of binary nn-pairs. ∎

We could have done all the work in this section with ℐf1{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{1}, the dual of ℐfn−3′{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-3}^{\prime}, and considered analogs of binary pairs where the conditions on the module would be 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-dual to the conditions on II in a binary pair. It turns out some of the constructions are more natural when working with ℐfn−3′{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-3}^{\prime} and binary pairs, so we have used that version in this exposition.

One can prove analogs of Theorem 4.7 for all ll-twisted binary forms. We define an kk-twisted binary nn-pair is an 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-algebra RR, an RR-module II, an exact sequence 0→Symn−3Q∗⊗(∧2Q)⊗−k→I→Q→00\rightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}Q)^{\otimes-k}\rightarrow I\rightarrow Q\rightarrow 0 such that QQ is a locally free rank 22 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module, and an isomorphism R/𝒪S≅Symn−2Q⊗(∧2Q)⊗kR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\cong\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\otimes(\wedge^{2}Q)^{\otimes k} that identifies the map R/𝒪S⊗Symn−3Q∗⊗(∧2Q)⊗−k→QR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}Q)^{\otimes-k}\rightarrow Q induced from the action of RR on II with the natural map Symn−2Q⊗(∧2Q)⊗k⊗Symn−3Q∗⊗(∧2Q)⊗−k→Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\otimes(\wedge^{2}Q)^{\otimes k}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{n-3}Q^{*}\otimes(\wedge^{2}Q)^{\otimes-k}\rightarrow Q. Given an ll-twisted binary nn-ic form, we have an (l+1)(l+1)-twisted binary pair from ℛf{\mathcal{R}_{f}}, ℐfn−3′{\mathcal{I}_{f}}_{n-3}^{\prime}, and the exact sequence from Equation (15).

For example, in a kk-twisted binary 33-pair we can see that I≅R⊗∧2Q⊗−kI\cong R\otimes\wedge^{2}Q^{\otimes-k}, by the same argument that we used to see II was a principal RR-module in a binary 33-pair. So, we see that II is determined uniquely by RR and QQ. However, since we have that R/𝒪S≅Q⊗(∧2Q)⊗kR/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\cong Q\otimes(\wedge^{2}Q)^{\otimes k}, we see that not all cubic algebras will appear as kk-twisted binary 33-pairs.

5 Further questions

For simplicity, we ask further questions over the base ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. One naturally wonders which rank nn rings appear in a binary pair. In other words, which rank nn rings have modules satisfying the conditions of a binary pair? When n=3n=3, we saw that the answer is all cubic rings, and each has a unique module and exact sequence that makes a binary pair. For n=4n=4, there is another characterization of the answer. In [21] it is shown that the quartic rings associated to binary quartic forms are exactly the quartic rings with monogenic cubic resolvents. The cubic resolvent is a certain integral model of the classical cubic resolvent field. Are there such connections with resolvents for higher nn?

Simon [17] asks which maximal orders are constructed from binary nn-ic forms. He defines the index of a form to be the index of its ring in the maximal order. He begins a program to compute all forms with a given index. For example, in the quartic case he uses elliptic curves to compute the forms of index 1 and a certain II and JJ (GL2⁡(ℤ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}({\mathbb{Z}}) invariants of a binary quartic form). Simon also shows that there are no index 1 forms with a root generating a cyclic extension of prime degree at least 5. In general, it would be very interesting to understand which maximal orders are associated to binary forms.

Appendix B Maps between locally free 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-modules

Let SS be a scheme. In this appendix we will give several basic facts about maps between locally free 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-modules.

Lemma B.1.

Let VV be a locally free 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}} module. We have (Symn⁡V)∗≅Symn⁡V∗(\operatorname{Sym}_{n}V)^{*}\cong\operatorname{Sym}^{n}V^{*}.

Lemma B.2.

Let VV be a locally free 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}} module. Inside of V⊗a+bV^{\otimes a+b} the submodule Syma+b⁡V\operatorname{Sym}_{a+b}V is a submodule of Syma⁡V⊗Symb⁡V\operatorname{Sym}_{a}V\otimes\operatorname{Sym}_{b}V. Thus we have a natural map

Syma+b⁡V→Syma⁡V⊗Symb⁡V,\operatorname{Sym}_{a+b}V\rightarrow\operatorname{Sym}_{a}V\otimes\operatorname{Sym}_{b}V,

which is injective.

Lemma B.3.

If LL is a locally free rank 1 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module and VV is a locally free rank nn 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module, then Symk⁡(V⊗L)≅Symk⁡V⊗L⊗k\operatorname{Sym}^{k}(V\otimes L)\cong\operatorname{Sym}^{k}V\otimes L^{\otimes k}.

Lemma B.4.

If VV is a locally free 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module of rank two then V⊗∧2V∗≅V∗V\otimes\wedge^{2}V^{*}\cong V^{*}.

Lemma B.5.

If QQ is any locally free rank 2 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module, we have the exact sequence

0⟶Symn−1⁡Q⟶Q⊗Symn−2⁡Q⟶Symn−3Q⊗∧2Q⟶0.q1q2⋯qn−1↦q1⊗q2⋯qn−1↦q2⋯qn−2⊗(qn−1∧q1)\begin{array}[]{ccccccccc}0&\longrightarrow&\operatorname{Sym}_{n-1}Q&\longrightarrow&Q\otimes\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q&\longrightarrow&\operatorname{Sym}_{n-3}Q\otimes\wedge^{2}Q&\longrightarrow&0.\\ &&q_{1}q_{2}\cdots q_{n-1}&\mapsto&q_{1}\otimes q_{2}\cdots q_{n-1}&\mapsto&q_{2}\cdots q_{n-2}\otimes(q_{n-1}\wedge q_{1})&&\end{array}
Proof.

We can check this sequence is exact and thus on free QQ generated by xx and yy. For a word ww in xx and yy, let sym⁡(w)\operatorname{sym}(w) denote the sum of all distinct permutations of ww. Then, a basis for Symn−1⁡Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n-1}Q is αk=sym⁡(xk​yn−1−k)\alpha_{k}=\operatorname{sym}(x^{k}y^{n-1-k}) for 0≤k≤n−10\leq k\leq n-1. A basis for Q⊗Symn−2⁡QQ\otimes\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q is given by

β0\displaystyle\beta_{0} =y⊗sym⁡(yn−2)\displaystyle=y\otimes\operatorname{sym}(y^{n-2})
βk\displaystyle\beta_{k} =x⊗sym⁡(xk−1​yn−1−k)+y⊗sym⁡(xk​yn−2−k)​ for ​1≤k≤n−2\displaystyle=x\otimes\operatorname{sym}(x^{k-1}y^{n-1-k})+y\otimes\operatorname{sym}(x^{k}y^{n-2-k})\text{ for }1\leq k\leq n-2
βn−1\displaystyle\beta_{n-1} =x⊗sym⁡(xn−2)\displaystyle=x\otimes\operatorname{sym}(x^{n-2})
γℓ\displaystyle\gamma_{\ell} =x⊗sym⁡(xℓ​yn−2−ℓ)​ for ​0≤ℓ≤n−3.\displaystyle=x\otimes\operatorname{sym}(x^{\ell}y^{n-2-\ell})\text{ for }0\leq\ell\leq n-3.

We see that in the sequence of the proposition, αi↦βi\alpha_{i}\mapsto\beta_{i} and the γℓ\gamma_{\ell} map to a basis of Symn−3Q⊗∧2Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n-3}Q\otimes\wedge^{2}Q. ∎

Lemma B.6.

Let RR be an 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-algebra, II be an RR-module, QQ be a locally free rank 2 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-module quotient of II, and ϕ\phi be an isomorphism of 𝒪S{\mathcal{O}_{S}}-modules ϕ:Symn−2⁡Q≅R/𝒪S\phi:\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\cong R/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}. If

Symn−1⁡Q⊗ker⁡(I→Q)⟶∧2Qq1⋯qn−1⊗k↦q1∧ϕ(q2⋯qn−1)∘k\begin{array}[]{ccc}\operatorname{Sym}_{n-1}Q\otimes\ker(I\rightarrow Q)&\longrightarrow&\wedge^{2}Q\\ q_{1}\cdots q_{n-1}\otimes k&\mapsto&q_{1}\wedge\phi(q_{2}\cdots q_{n-1})\circ k\end{array}

is the zero map, then

Symn⁡Q⟶∧2Qq1⋯qn↦q1∧ϕ(q2⋯qn−1)∘qn~\begin{array}[]{ccc}\operatorname{Sym}_{n}Q&\longrightarrow&\wedge^{2}Q\\ q_{1}\cdots q_{n}&\mapsto&q_{1}\wedge\phi(q_{2}\cdots q_{n-1})\circ\tilde{q_{n}}\end{array}

is well-defined. Here the ∘\circ denotes the action of RR on II followed by the quotient to QQ and q~\tilde{q} denotes a fixed splitting Q→IQ\rightarrow I. In particular the map SymnQ→∧2Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n}Q\rightarrow\wedge^{2}Q does not depend on the choice of this splitting.

Proof.

Since Symn−1⁡Q⊂Q⊗Symn−2⁡Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n-1}Q\subset Q\otimes\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q as submodules of Q⊗nQ^{\otimes n} (see Lemma B.2), the first map Symn−1Q⊗ker(I→Q)→∧2Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n-1}Q\otimes\ker(I\rightarrow Q)\rightarrow\wedge^{2}Q is well-defined. For a given choice of splittings Symn−2⁡Q→R\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\rightarrow R and Q→IQ\rightarrow I, consider the following commutative diagram.

To investigate the effect of a different splitting Q→IQ\rightarrow I on the map SymnQ→∧2Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n}Q\rightarrow\wedge^{2}Q, we take the route on the right hand side of the diagram. The difference between the composite maps from two different splittings will land in the submodule Symn−1⁡Q⊗ker⁡(I→Q)\operatorname{Sym}_{n-1}Q\otimes\ker(I\rightarrow Q) of the Symn−1⁡Q⊗I\operatorname{Sym}_{n-1}Q\otimes I term, and thus be zero in the final map by the hypothesis of the lemma.

To investigate the effect of a different splitting Symn−2⁡Q≅R/𝒪S→R\operatorname{Sym}_{n-2}Q\cong R/{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\rightarrow R on the map SymnQ→∧2Q\operatorname{Sym}_{n}Q\rightarrow\wedge^{2}Q, we take the route on the left hand side of the diagram. The difference between the maps from the different splittings will land in the submodule 𝒪S⊗Sym2⁡Q{\mathcal{O}_{S}}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}_{2}Q of the R⊗Sym2⁡QR\otimes\operatorname{Sym}_{2}Q term, and it is easy to see that the difference will be zero in the composite map. ∎
